# Robust Mean Estimation With Auxiliary Samples

**Authors:** Barron Han∗, Danil Akhtiamov∗, Reza Ghane∗, Babak Hassibi Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering Caltech Pasadena, California ∗Equal contribution Email: {bshan, dakhtiam, rghanekh, hassibi}@caltech.edu

## Abstract

In data-driven learning and inference tasks, the high cost of acquiring samples from the target distribution often limits performance. A common strategy to mitigate this challenge is to augment the limited target samples with data from a more accessible "auxiliary" distribution. This paper establishes fundamental limits of this approach by analyzing the improvement in the mean square error (MSE) when estimating the mean of the target distribution. Using the Wasserstein-2 metric to quantify the distance between distributions, we derive expressions for the worst-case MSE when samples are drawn (with labels) from both a target distribution and an auxiliary distribution within a specified Wasserstein-2 distance from the target distribution. We explicitly characterize the achievable MSE and the optimal estimator in terms of the problem dimension, the number of samples from the target and auxiliary distributions, the Wasserstein-2 distance, and the covariance of the target distribution. We note that utilizing samples from the auxiliary distribution effectively improves the MSE when the squared radius of the Wasserstein-2 uncertainty ball is small compared to the variance of the true distribution and the number of samples from the true distribution is limited. Numerical simulations in the Gaussian location model illustrate the theoretical findings.

## I Introduction and Motivation

While modern data-driven techniques and deep learning models continue to achieve remarkable success in various inference tasks, access to training data remains a significant challenge. Often, acquiring data from the true (target) distribution is expensive or time-consuming. One technique is to augment data from the true distribution with data from auxiliary distributions that closely approximate the target distribution. For example, while collecting real-world data for self-driving vehicles is costly, simulated environments provide a more affordable alternative that can still be utilized for learning and inference. More explicitly, consider machine learning model training, where $\mathbf{W}$ are the network weights, $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ are the data and labels, respectively. We often approximate the true expected loss: $\mathbb{E}\left[l(\mathbf{W};\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}\right)]$ with respect to the underlying distribution of the data with the empirical loss $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}l(\mathbf{W};x_{i},y_{i})$ . Auxiliary data $\mathbf{Z}$ can be used to complement the empirical loss and provide a better estimate of the true expected loss. Another promising application involves employing the output of predictive or generative models to improve performance in inference tasks. For example, [1] studies statistical methods for inference when a small amount of true data is supplemented by a large number of AI generated predictions. Data from generative models have been shown to improve the generalization capabilities of classifiers such as in [2].

This paper is motivated by the following questions: How closely must an auxiliary distribution approximate the target distribution for its samples to be useful in making inferences about the true distribution? How can we design optimal estimators for the statistics of the true distribution using samples from both the true and auxiliary distributions? Can we establish worst-case performance guarantees for statistical estimators when samples are drawn from an adversarially chosen auxiliary distribution? We aim to address such questions by analyzing the fundamental problem of mean estimation.

Robust estimation using auxiliary data has a rich history in prior literature. The “data contamination" setting considers the auxiliary data as contaminated samples from the true distribution. The samples are not labeled so it is unknown in advance which data points are contaminated. In his seminal work, Huber introduced the $\epsilon$ -contamination model in which samples are drawn from a mixture distribution $(1-\epsilon)\mathbb{P}+\epsilon\mathbb{Q}$ where $\mathbb{P}$ is the true distribution for the data and $\mathbb{Q}$ represents a contaminated distribution. Moreover, the same article studies the case where $\mathbb{P}$ is normal, with $\mathbb{Q}$ chosen within a total variation (TV) ball centered at $\mathbb{P}$ . Variations of Huber’s $\epsilon$ -contamination problem such as [3] consider various metrics to measure the distance between the true distribution $\mathbb{P}$ and contaminated distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ , including the TV, Kolmogorov, Levy, and Prokhov distances. We refer to [4] for an overview of robust statistics. Our problem setting differs from Huber’s primarily since it is known a priori which samples belong to the true distribution and which belong to the auxiliary distribution. Consequently, the samples from the auxiliary distribution can only help inference – we can always choose to ignore the auxiliary samples. Our proposed setting more closely models data augmentation problems in modern machine learning and inference.

Another setting from past work involves all samples originating from a shifted distribution, where the objective is to design statistical estimators that remain robust to such distribution shifts. Wasserstein distances often lead to tractable formulations for such problems, as they provide a natural measure of distance between the true and shifted distributions [5, 6, 7]. An advantage of the Wasserstein distance is that it imposes minimal assumptions on the underlying noise distribution. For instance, the $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ distance is symmetric and well defined even for distributions with nonoverlapping support, properties not shared by the KL divergence. Moreover, the Wasserstein distance plays a fundamental role in fields such as optimal transport and is used for modeling discrepancies between an empirical distribution, derived from observed samples, and the true distribution.

For example, [8], [9], and [10] examine robust mean estimation in scenarios where samples are drawn from the worst-case shifted distribution within a Wasserstein neighborhood of the target distribution. Unlike the contamination model, this framework assumes that the samples are generated entirely from the shifted distribution. [8] constructs estimators for this problem by projecting the empirical distribution onto a well-behaved family of distributions that contains the true distribution. For Wasserstein or TV distribution shifts, [8] shows that this method asymptotically achieves the optimal error. [9] considers robust mean estimation, covariance estimation, and linear regression under distribution shifts. For mean estimation, which is the subject of this paper, they propose an estimator motivated by generative adverserial networks, and demonstrate that when the true distribution is Gaussian or elliptical, the estimator can achieve the optimal min-max $L_{2}$ estimation error. [10] extend the prior framework by considering distribution shifts that can be independent or jointly shifted across data points. For the mean estimation problem with mean square loss, [10] determined the exact min-max risk, the worst-case Wasserstein shift, and the least squares estimator.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we formalize the auxiliary data model, which produces $n$ samples from the true distribution and $N$ samples from an auxiliary distribution, and the distributionally robust optimization objective for mean estimation. In Section III, we present our main results. We reduce the maximization for the worst-case MSE over all true and auxiliary distributions to an optimization over only their first and second moment statistics. By reducing the problem to Gaussians without loss of generality, we determine the optimal robust estimator, worst-case auxiliary distribution, and the min-max mean estimation error. We propose a few variations to the objective and present the optimal estimators for each case separately. In Section IV we present the proofs. Finally, in Section V we demonstrate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations for the performance of the proposed estimator in a Gaussian location setting.

## II Problem Formulation

We start with the definition of the Wasserstein- $p$ ( $\mathcal{W}_{p}$ ) distance.

#### Definition 1.

For two probability measures $\mathbb{P}_{1}$ and $\mathbb{P}_{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with finite $p$ th moment, the Wasserstein distance is defined as

$$ \displaystyle W_{p}(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2})=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2})}\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{2}\|_{p}^{p}\gamma(d\mathbf{x}_{1},d\mathbf{x}_{2})\Bigr)^{\frac{1}{p}} $$

Where $\Pi$ is the set of all couplings on $\mathbb{P}_{1}\times\mathbb{P}_{2}$ such that for each $\gamma\in\Pi$ , $\pi_{i\#}\gamma=\mathbb{P}_{i}$ .

In this work, we focus on the $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ distance, where $p=2$ in (1). Consider two datasets, $\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ and $\{\mathbf{Z}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , where $\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are sampled i.i.d. from an unknown distribution $\mathbb{P}$ , and $\{\mathbf{Z}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ are sampled i.i.d. from another unknown distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ . We know in advance that the distributions satisfy $\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon>0$ . In practice, $\mathbb{P}$ represents the distribution to be learned, while $\mathbb{Q}$ serves as a surrogate for $\mathbb{P}$ . The natural question arises: What is the optimal way to estimate the mean of $\mathbb{P}$ , denoted by $\bm{\mu}_{X}$ , using an estimator trained on both $\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ and $\{\mathbf{Z}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , given $\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon$ ? This question has motivated work such as [1], but their setting assumes that the true data come in pairs $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ where $\mathbf{X}$ are features and $\mathbf{Y}$ are labels, and the goal is to utilize additional features $\bar{\mathbf{X}}$ and the predictions, $\bar{\mathbf{Y}}$ , of some unknown predictor as auxiliary samples to estimate with confidence some statistic on the underlying distribution of $\mathbf{Y}$ .

Furthermore, we assume that $N\gg 1$ capturing the case when sampling from $\mathbf{Z}$ is much cheaper than from $\mathbf{X}$ and that the Frobenius norm of the covariance matrix of $\mathbf{X}\sim\mathbb{P}$ , denoted by $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}$ , is bounded below by $\delta^{2}$ , which effectively imposes a lower bound on the uncertainty in $\mathbf{X}$ . Under these assumptions, our goal is to design an estimator $f$ that is robust to the choice of the true distribution $\mathbb{P}$ and also any auxiliary distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ in the $\epsilon$ -neighborhood of $\mathbb{P}$ . The optimal $f$ achieves the min-max rates:

$$ R^{*}=\min_{f}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}}\|f(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z})-\bm{\mu}_{X}\|^{2}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}. $$

A normalization factor such as $|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}|_{F}$ is necessary. Without it, for example, setting $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}=c\mathbf{I}_{d}$ with $c\to\infty$ causes the objective to diverge to infinity. This requirement also motivates the constraint $|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}$ , which ensures that the denominator remains bounded away from zero. Alternative normalization factors, such as $\text{Tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})$ or $|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}|_{op}$ , are also viable and considered in Section III. Practically, the objective represents a ratio (up to a constant factor) between the MSE of the estimator $f$ , and the error of an estimator that utilizes samples from the true distribution. For instance, the sample mean from the true distribution achieves a MSE of $\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})$ . We make the following linearity assumption on the estimator:

#### Assumption 1.

(Linear estimator structure) For the objectives in (2), we assume the estimator, $f$ , is linear with respect to the data $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z}$ and of the form:

$$ f(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{A}\frac{\sum\mathbf{X}_{i}}{n}+\mathbf{B}\frac{\sum\mathbf{Z}_{j}}{N} $$

where $\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}$ are constant matrices to determine.

## III Main results

Using the structure of the linear estimator from Assumption 1, (2) can be reformulated as (3a). Similarly, we consider variations of the objective by normalizing using the trace and operator norms in (3b) and (3c).

$$ \displaystyle R_{F}^{*} \displaystyle=\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\\
\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}}\|\mathbf{A}\frac{\sum\mathbf{X}_{i}}{n}+\mathbf{B}\frac{\sum\mathbf{Z}_{j}}{N}-\bm{\mu}_{X}\|^{2}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}, \displaystyle R_{\mathrm{Tr}}^{*} \displaystyle=\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\\
\mathrm{Tr}{(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}\geq\delta^{2}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}}\|\mathbf{A}\frac{\sum\mathbf{X}_{i}}{n}+\mathbf{B}\frac{\sum\mathbf{Z}_{j}}{N}-\bm{\mu}_{X}\|^{2}}{\mathrm{Tr}{(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}}, \displaystyle R_{op}^{*} \displaystyle=\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\\
|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}|_{op}\geq\delta^{2}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}}\|\mathbf{A}\frac{\sum\mathbf{X}_{i}}{n}+\mathbf{B}\frac{\sum\mathbf{Z}_{j}}{N}-\bm{\mu}_{X}\|^{2}}{|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}|_{op}}. $$

First, we establish a lemma claiming that (3) is sensitive only to the first and second moment statistics of the true distribution $\mathbb{P}$ and the auxiliary distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Lemma 1.

(Reduction to Gaussians) Consider the optimizations in (3). Without loss of generality, we can take

$$ \mathbb{P}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}),\quad\mathbb{Q}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}). $$

#### Proof.

The objective (3a) can be expanded as:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}} \displaystyle\frac{\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}{(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}+\frac{1}{N}\text{Tr}{(\mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{B}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}})}+\|\mathbf{A}\bm{\mu}_{X}+\mathbf{B}\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}\|^{2}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}, $$

where $\bm{\mu}_{Z}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{Z}$ denote the mean and covariance matrix of $\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathbb{Q}$ respectively.

Denote

$$ \bar{\mathbb{P}}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})~~~\mbox{and}~~~\bar{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}) $$

Note that, if $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ belong to the feasibility set of (4), then so do $\bar{\mathbb{P}}$ and $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ because $\mathcal{W}_{2}(\bar{\mathbb{P}},\bar{\mathbb{Q}})\leq\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})$ according to Theorem 2.1 in [11]. Note, moreover, that since the objective of (4) depends only on the first and second order statistics of $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ , the objective does not change if we replace $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ by $\bar{\mathbb{P}}$ and $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ respectively. Hence, we can take $\mathbb{P}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})$ and $\mathbb{Q}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}})$ without loss of generality, which in turn implies:

$$ \mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})^{2}=\|\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}\|^{2}+\mathrm{Tr}\left(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}-2(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\frac{1}{2}})^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) $$

∎

We arrive at our main theorems, which presents the optimal estimators for (3) and the optimal values of the objectives.

#### Theorem 1.

(Optimal estimator for (3a)) The optimal estimator is given by

$$ \mathbf{A}=s\mathbf{I},\ \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}, $$

where

$$ s=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N}+\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}}{\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}+\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}}. $$

The optimal value of the objective:

$$ R_{F}^{*}=\frac{\sqrt{d}(\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\sqrt{d}+N)}{\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\sqrt{d}(n+N)+\epsilon^{2}nN}, $$

where $n$ is the number of samples from the true distribution, $N$ is the number of samples from the auxiliary distribution, $d$ is the problem dimension, and $\epsilon$ is the $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ uncertainty radius.

#### Theorem 2.

(Optimal estimator for (3b)) The optimal estimator is given by

$$ \mathbf{A}=s\mathbf{I},\ \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A} $$

where

$$ s=\frac{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{1}{N}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{N}},\quad\text{and}\quad R_{\mathrm{Tr}}^{*}=\frac{\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}+N}{\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}(n+N)+nN}, $$

with $n,N,\delta,\epsilon$ defined in Theorem 1.

#### Theorem 3.

(Optimal estimator for 3c) The optimal estimator is given by

$$ \mathbf{A}=s\mathbf{I},\ \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A} $$

where

$$ s=\frac{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{d}{N}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{d}{n}+\frac{d}{N}},\quad\text{and}\quad R_{op}^{*}=\frac{d(\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}d+N)}{\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}d(n+N)+nN}, $$

with $n,N,\delta,\epsilon$ defined in Theorem 1.

The key insight from Theorems 1, 2 and 3 is that normalizing the objective using various matrix norms on $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}$ does not alter the structure of the optimal estimator or the interactions between $n$ , $N$ , $\delta$ , and $\epsilon$ in the optimal weighting constant, $s$ , or the optimal objective value, $R^{*}$ , except for introducing a different dependence on the dimension of the problem $d$ .

In general, the weighting factor approaches $s\to 1$ , implying the estimate becomes more sensitive to the true samples while disregarding the auxiliary samples, if $\epsilon^{2}\gg\frac{\delta^{2}}{n}$ . This condition suggests that the auxiliary distribution provides a poor approximation of the true distribution, and the mean estimation task is relatively easy using only the true samples.

Let $R^{*}$ be the optimal rate in Theorem 2. The expression

$$ nR^{*}=\frac{\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}+N}{\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}(1+\frac{N}{n})+N} $$

is the ratio between the worst-case MSE of the robust estimator and the MSE of the sample mean from the true distribution. This ratio is small when the uncertainty in the true distribution (parametrized by $\delta^{2}$ ) is large compared to the square of the $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ radius $\epsilon$ . In fact, $\frac{\delta^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}$ should be on the order of $N$ , the number of auxiliary samples. Further, $\frac{N}{n}$ should be large, indicating that the number of true samples is relatively limited.

## IV Proof of Theorem 1

We provide a detailed proof of Theorem 1. The proofs for Theorems 2 and 3 require slight algebraic modifications and are excluded for brevity.

#### Proof.

Note that (4) is unbounded unless $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}$ . Indeed, fix arbitrary $\mathbf{A},\ \mathbf{B},\ \bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}},$ and $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ and take $\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}=\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ align with the principal singular direction of $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{I}$ satisfying $\|\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}\|\to\infty$ and such that (5) is upper-bounded by $\epsilon$ . We have

$$ \|\mathbf{A}\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}+\mathbf{B}\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}\|^{2}=\|(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{I})\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}\|^{2}\to\infty\\
 $$

unless $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{I}=0$ .

From the above remark, (4) takes the following form:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A}}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}}\frac{\|(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}})\|^{2}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}+ \displaystyle\frac{\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}{(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}+\frac{1}{N}\text{Tr}{((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}})}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}. $$

Since $\|(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})(\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}})\|^{2}$ is the only term in the objective that depends on the direction of $\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ and $\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})$ depends only on the norm of $\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ as well, it is clear that $\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ will align with the principal singular direction of $\mathbf{A}$ and we obtain the following:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A}}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}}\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}\|\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}}-\bm{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}}\|^{2}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}+ \displaystyle\frac{\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}{(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}+\frac{1}{N}\text{Tr}{((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}})}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}. $$

Hence, the constraint $\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})=\epsilon$ is active and we arrive at:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A}}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}} \displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}(\epsilon^{2}-\text{Tr}{(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}-2(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\frac{1}{2}})^{\frac{1}{2}}))}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}+ \displaystyle\frac{\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}{(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}+\frac{1}{N}\text{Tr}{((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}})}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}} $$

Define $\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}=(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\frac{1}{2}})^{\frac{1}{2}}$ , then $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}=\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{2}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ and (16) becomes,

$$ \displaystyle \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A}}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}} \displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}(\epsilon^{2}-\text{Tr}{(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}+\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{2}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}}))}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}+ \displaystyle\frac{\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}{(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}+\frac{1}{N}\text{Tr}{((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{2}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}})}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}} $$

Let us take the matrix derivative by $\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ and equate it to zero. Note that it does not take the constraint $\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}\succ 0$ into account but as we will see the solution of the corresponding KKT conditions will turn out to be positive definite by itself:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{2}{N}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}} \displaystyle-\sigma_{max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}(2\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-1}\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}-2\mathbf{I})=0. $$

We recover $\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}=\sigma_{max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}\cdot\Big(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\big(\sigma_{max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2} \displaystyle-\frac{1}{N}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\big)\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Big)^{-1} $$

We deduce that as $N\to\infty$ , $\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ uniformly converges to $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}$ in the operator norm. Hence, for large enough $N$ , $\tilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{Z}}\approx\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}$ implying $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}}\approx\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}$ and we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A}}\max_{\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})\leq\epsilon,\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}\geq\delta^{2}} \displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}\epsilon^{2}+\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}{\big(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\big)}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}} \displaystyle+\frac{\frac{1}{N}\text{Tr}{((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}}{\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}}. $$

Hence, $\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}$ aligns with $\frac{\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}}{n}+\frac{(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})}{N}$ , $\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}=\delta^{2}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{A}}\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{I})^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\|\frac{\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A}}{n}+\frac{(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})}{N}\|_{F}. $$

Use the singular value decomposition $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}$ , where $\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are unitary and $\mathbf{S}=\text{diag}(s_{1},\dots,s_{d})$ where $s_{1}\geq s_{2}\dots\geq s_{d}\geq 0$ . The objective (20) decomposes as

$$ \displaystyle\min_{s_{1}\geq s_{2}\geq\dots\geq s_{d}\geq 0} \displaystyle\frac{\max\{(s_{1}-1)^{2},(s_{d}-1)^{2}\}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{\sum_{i}\left(\frac{s_{i}^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s_{i})^{2}}{N}\right)^{2}} $$

Now note that for $d>i>1$ the optimization in $s_{i}$ is quadratic with a single constraint $s_{1}\geq s_{i}\geq s_{d}$ and we have:

$$ s_{i}=s:=\begin{cases}&\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}\text{ if }s_{1}\geq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}\geq s_{d}\\
&s_{1}\text{ if }s_{1}<\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}\\
&s_{d}\text{ if }s_{d}>\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}\\
\end{cases} $$

Consider the cases above one by one:

$\bullet$ If $s_{1}\geq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}\geq s_{d}$ , then $s_{d}=1+\frac{N}{n}=s$ as well because this choice of $s_{d}$ minimizes both $(1-s_{d})^{2}$ and $\frac{s_{d}^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s_{d})^{2}}{N}$ under the given constraints and $\max\{(s_{1}-1)^{2},(s_{d}-1)^{2}\}=(s_{d}-1)^{2}$ because the optimal $s_{d}\leq s_{1}\leq 1$ . Hence, (21) becomes:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{s_{1}\geq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}}\frac{N^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}(n+N)^{2}}+\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s_{1})^{2}}{N}\right)^{2}+\frac{d-1}{(n+N)^{2}}} $$

Therefore, the optimal $s_{1}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}$ as well, $\mathbf{A}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}\mathbf{I}$ and the value of the objective (21) equals

$$ \displaystyle\frac{N^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{(n+N)^{2}\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n+N}=\frac{1}{n+N}\left(\frac{N^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{(n+N)\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d}\right) $$

$\bullet$ If $s_{d}\geq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}$ , then as discussed earlier $s_{2}=\dots=s_{d-1}=:s=s_{d}$ , and (21) simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\min_{s_{1}\geq s\geq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}}\frac{\max\{(s_{1}-1)^{2},(s-1)^{2}\}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+ \displaystyle\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_{1}^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s_{1})^{2}}{N}\right)^{2}+(d-1)(\frac{s^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s)^{2}}{N})^{2}} $$

Hence, $s_{1}=s_{d}$ as well, because otherwise resetting $s_{1}:=s$ would decrease the first term and not change the second and we arrive at:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{s\geq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}}\frac{(s-1)^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d}\left(\frac{s^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s)^{2}}{N}\right) $$

$\bullet$ If $s_{1}\leq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}$ , similarly to the previous case we arrive at the following:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{s\leq\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{n}}}\frac{(s-1)^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d}\left(\frac{s^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s)^{2}}{N}\right) $$

Combining (25) and (26) altogether into one objective, we arrive at:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{s}\frac{(s-1)^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d}\left(\frac{s^{2}}{n}+\frac{(1-s)^{2}}{N}\right) $$

Hence, $s=\frac{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}}$ , $\mathbf{A}=s\mathbf{I}$ and the corresponding value of the objective is equal to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{(\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N})^{2}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}+(\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N})\frac{d}{n^{2}}}{(\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n})^{2}}=\frac{(\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N})\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}} \displaystyle=\frac{(\frac{\epsilon^{2}N}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d})\sqrt{d}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}nN}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d}(n+N)}=\frac{1}{n+N}\frac{(\frac{\epsilon^{2}N}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d})\sqrt{d}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}nN}{\delta^{2}(n+N)}+\sqrt{d}} $$

(28) is upper-bounded by (23). It suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{(\frac{\epsilon^{2}N}{\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d})\sqrt{d}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}nN}{\delta^{2}(n+N)}+\sqrt{d}}\leq\frac{N^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{(n+N)\delta^{2}}+\sqrt{d} $$

Simplifying the expression:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{\delta^{2}}\frac{N^{2}}{n+N}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\frac{\epsilon^{2}nN}{\delta^{2}(n+N)}+\sqrt{d}}\leq\frac{N^{2}\epsilon^{2}}{(n+N)\delta^{2}}, $$

implying that (28) is the optimal solution to (14). ∎

## V Numerical Experiments

To showcase our theoretical predictions, we conduct a numerical experiment as follows. We take $\mathbb{P}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\mathbb{P}},\sigma\mathbf{I}_{d})$ and $\mathbb{Q}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\mathbb{Q}},\sigma\mathbf{I}_{d})$ to be two $d$ -dimensional Gaussian distributions with different means and the same scalar covariance satisfying $\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})^{2}=\|\mu_{\mathbb{P}}-\mu_{\mathbb{Q}}\|^{2}=\epsilon^{2}$ and $\|\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}=\delta^{2}$ and fix $\epsilon=\delta=1$ . We take the dimension $d=200$ and generate $n=20$ samples $\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n}$ from $\mathbb{P}$ and $N=1000$ samples $\mathbf{z}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{z}_{N}$ from $\mathbb{Q}$ . We then compare the average performances of three predictors for the "true" mean $\mathbb{P}$ : averaging over the "true" data $\frac{\mathbf{x}_{1}+\dots+\mathbf{x}_{n}}{n}$ plotted in green, averaging over all data $\frac{\mathbf{x}_{1}+\dots+\mathbf{x}_{n}+\mathbf{z}_{1}+\dots+\mathbf{z}_{N}}{n+N}$ plotted in blue, and the optimal weighted average from Theorem 1 plotted in red. As expected, the optimal estimator achieves lower error compared to both naive averaging of all the samples or averaging of only the samples from the true distribution. When the $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ is small, the optimal estimator essentially averages all the samples. As the $\mathcal{W}_{2}$ distance, $\epsilon$ grows large, the optimal error approaches the error of the sample average from the true distribution.

*Fig. 1: MSE of optimal estimator from Theorem 1.*

## VI Conclusion

We suggest a new framework for mean estimation using samples from both true and auxiliary distributions and find the worst-case optimal linear mean estimator. We show that incorporating auxiliary data for estimation always improves performance compared to just averaging over the true distribution. However, the improvement is marginal unless one of the following conditions holds: the auxiliary data distribution matches the original one closely, the original data is very noisy or there is a very limited number of samples from the original distribution.

Potential directions for future work include extending the analyses to other statistical distances, such as $W_{p}$ -distances for $p\neq 2$ and the KL-divergence, and exploring potential practical applications of the introduced framework.

# A Novel Gaussian Min-Max Theorem and its Applications

**Authors:** Danil Akhtiamov∗, Reza Ghane∗, Nithin K Varma and Babak Hassibi Affiliation: Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Pasadena, CA, USA Email: {dakhtiam, rghanekh, nkanumur, hassibi}@caltech.edu Affiliation: Affiliation: David Bosch∗ Affiliation: Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology Gothenburg, Sweden Email: davidbos@chalmers.se

## Abstract

A celebrated result by Gordon allows one to compare the min-max behavior of two Gaussian processes if certain inequality conditions are met. The consequences of this result include the Gaussian min-max (GMT) and convex Gaussian min-max (CGMT) theorems which have had far-reaching implications in high-dimensional statistics, machine learning, non-smooth optimization, and signal processing. Both theorems rely on a pair of Gaussian processes, first identified by Slepian, that satisfy Gordon’s comparison inequalities. In this paper, we identify a new pair of Gaussian processes satisfying these inequalities. The resulting theorems extend the classical GMT and CGMT Theorems from the case where the underlying Gaussian matrix in the primary process has iid rows to where it has independent but non-identically-distributed ones. The new CGMT is applied to the problems of multi-source Gaussian regression, as well as to binary classification of general Gaussian mixture models.

#### Index Terms:

## I Introduction and Motivation

Assume the matrix $G\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d}$ , the vectors $g\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ and $h\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ , and the scalar $\gamma$ all have i.i.d ${\cal N}(0,1)$ , i.e., standard normal entries. Then, considering deterministic vectors $w\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ and $v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ , belonging to some sets ${\cal S}_{w}$ and ${\cal S}_{v}$ , we can obtain the following pair of Gaussian processes

$$ X_{wv}=v^{T}Gw+\gamma\|w\|_{2}\|v\|_{2}~~~\mbox{and}~~~Y_{wv}=\|v\|_{2}g^{T}w+\|w\|_{2}h^{T}v, $$

which we will refer to as a Slepian pair (Slepian,, 1962). For such Slepian pairs, it can be readily shown that

$$ \mathbb{E}X_{wv}X_{w^{\prime}v^{\prime}}-\mathbb{E}Y_{wv}Y_{w^{\prime}v^{\prime}}=\left(\|w\|_{2}\|w^{\prime}\|_{2}-w^{T}w^{\prime})(\|v\|_{2}\|v^{\prime}\|_{2}-v^{T}v^{\prime}\right) $$

By recalling Cauchy-Schwarz, this implies that the processes $X_{wv}$ and $Y_{wv}$ satisfy the following (so-called) comparison inequalities

$$ \mathbb{E}X_{wv}X_{w^{\prime}v^{\prime}}\leq\mathbb{E}Y_{wv}Y_{w^{\prime}v^{\prime}}~~~\mbox{and}~~~\mathbb{E}X_{wv}X_{wv^{\prime}}\geq\mathbb{E}Y_{wv}Y_{wv^{\prime}} $$

For Gaussian processes that satisfy the inequalities (1), Gordon, (1985) showed that it is possible to relate

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\min_{w\in{\cal S}_{w}}\max_{v\in{\cal S}_{v}}X_{wv}\geq\psi(w,v)\right) $$

to

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\min_{w\in{\cal S}_{w}}\max_{v\in{\cal S}_{v}}Y_{wv}\geq\psi(w,v)\right), $$

for any function $\psi(w,v)$ . We refer the reader to the next section for more details. This remarkable result allows one to infer properties of a so-called primary optimization (PO)

$$ \min_{w\in{\cal S}_{w}}\max_{v\in{\cal S}_{v}}v^{T}Gw+\psi(w,v) $$

in terms of a simpler so-called auxiliary optimization (AO)

$$ \min_{w\in{\cal S}_{w}}\max_{v\in{\cal S}_{v}}\|v\|_{2}g^{T}w+\|w\|_{2}h^{T}v+\psi(w,v). $$

This is the gist of the Gaussian min-max (GMT) (Gordon,, 1988) and convex Gaussian min-max (CGMT) (Thrampoulidis et al.,, 2014) theorems. The CGMT, in particular, has found numerous recent applications where, along with statistical physics-inspired methods, such as the replica method and approximate message passing (AMP), it has been used to derive sharp bounds on the performance of a variety of problems in high-dimensional statistics, machine learning, non-smooth convex optimization, and signal processing (e.g., (Stojnic,, 2013; Salehi et al.,, 2019; Akhtiamov et al.,, 2023; Mignacco et al.,, 2020; Thrampoulidis et al.,, 2018; Javanmard and Soltanolkotabi,, 2022; Montanari et al.,, 2019; Salehi et al.,, 2020; Aolaritei et al.,, 2023; Zhou et al.,, 2024))

In this paper, we identify a novel pair of Gaussian processes that satisfy Gordon’s inequalities (1). This in turn allows for comparison between a new primary and auxiliary optimization, which, as we show below, can express problems which the known CGMT can not analyze.

The new pair of processes are as follows:

$$ X_{w,v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\left[v_{\ell}^{T}G_{\ell}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\gamma_{\ell}\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}\right], $$

and

$$ Y_{w,v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\left[\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}\right], $$

where $\{G_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{\ell}\times d}\}_{\ell=1}^{k}$ , $\{g_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\}_{\ell=1}^{k}$ , $\{h_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{\ell}}\}_{\ell=1}^{k}$ and $\{\gamma_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}\}_{\ell=1}^{k}$ all have i.i.d ${\cal N}(0,1)$ standard normal entries and $\Sigma_{\ell}^{1/2}$ are $d\times d$ are positive semi-definite (PSD) matrices.

The remainder of the paper is devoted to obtaining the CGMT counterpart of the above pair of Gaussian random processes and to applying this novel CGMT to analyze two specific problems: firstly, multi-source Gaussian regression and, secondarily, binary classification of general Gaussian mixture models. We note that neither problem lends itself to analysis via the conventional CGMT.

## II Related works

We would like to highlight two recent works that provide other interesting examples of Gaussian Processes satisfying (1). Dhifallah and Lu, (2021) introduce another generalization of the Convex Gaussian Min-Max Theorem that they use to analyze the effects of noise injection on the generalization performance of Random Feature Models. Jain et al., (2024) apply Gaussian Comparison Inequalities to analyze a pair of processes that arises in their analysis of the performance of linear models trained on a mixture of true and synthetic data. An interested reader can see Remarks 2 and 1 in Section IV for more details.

## III Preliminaries

### III-A Gordon’s comparison inequality for Gaussian Processes

Introduced by Gordon in his landmark paper (Gordon,, 1985), the following comparison inequality is instrumental in proving the main results of our paper:

#### Theorem 1 (Gordon’s comparison inequality Gordon, (1985)).

Let $I$ and $J$ be two finite sets and $\{X_{ij}\}_{i\in I,j\in J}$ , $\{Y_{ij}\}_{i\in I,j\in J}$ be two real valued centered Gaussian processes, which satisfy the following conditions:

- 1. $\mathbb{E}X_{ij}^{2}=\mathbb{E}Y_{ij}^{2}$ for all $i\in I,j\in J$

- 2. $\mathbb{E}X_{ij}X_{ij^{\prime}}\geq\mathbb{E}Y_{ij}Y_{ij^{\prime}}$ for all $i\in I,j,j^{\prime}\in J$

- 3. $\mathbb{E}X_{ij}X_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\leq\mathbb{E}Y_{ij}Y_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}$ for all $i\neq i^{\prime}\in I,j,j^{\prime}\in J$

Let $\{t_{ij}\}_{i\in I,j\in J}$ be an arbitrary sequence of real numbers indexed by $(i,j)\in I\times J$ . Then the following inequality holds:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[Y_{ij}\geq t_{ij}]\right)\geq\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[X_{ij}\geq t_{ij}]\right) $$

Now, let $G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ , $g\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $h\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ all have i.i.d $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ components, $I$ and $J$ be finite sets and $\{w_{i}\}_{i\in I}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $\{u_{j}\}_{j\in J}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be arbitrary discrete subsets. It was first observed in Gordon, (1988) that the following processes satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 1:

$$ \displaystyle Y_{ij}=v_{j}^{T}Gw_{i}+\gamma\|w_{i}\|_{2}\|v_{j}\|_{2} \displaystyle X_{ij}=\|v_{j}\|_{2}g^{T}w_{i}+\|w_{i}\|_{2}h^{T}v_{j} $$

By making an appropriate choice for the values of $\{t_{ij}\}_{i\in I,j\in J}$ , and by proving that finite discrete subsets can be extended to compact sets, the following theorem can be proven. This theorem provides a probabilistic upper bound on the value of a more complicated optimization problem $\Phi$ , which extends $Y_{ij}$ , being larger than some threshold $t$ , by means of the same quantity for an alternative optimization $\phi$ , which extends $X_{ij}$ . The alternative problem, $\phi$ , is in general easier to analyze.

#### Theorem 2.

Let $\mathcal{S}_{w}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{S}_{v}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be compact sets and $\psi(w,v):\mathcal{S}_{w}\times\mathcal{S}_{v}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function. Let $G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ , $g\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $h\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ all have i.i.d $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ components, and be independent of each other. Then letting

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(G,\gamma):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}v^{T}Gw+\gamma\|w\|_{2}\|v\|_{2}+\psi(w,v) \displaystyle\phi(g,h):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\|v\|_{2}g^{T}w+\|w\|_{2}h^{T}v+\psi(w,v) $$

We have for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi(G,\gamma)<t)\leq\mathbb{P}(\phi(g,h)<t) $$

The theorem above has an immediate corollary:

#### Corollary 1 (Gaussian Min-Max Theorem).

Assume the same setup as Theorem 2. Then letting

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(G):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}v^{T}Gw+\psi(w,v) \displaystyle\phi(g,h):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\|v\|_{2}g^{T}w+\|w\|_{2}h^{T}v+\psi(w,v) $$

we have for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi(G,\gamma)<t)\leq 2\mathbb{P}(\phi(g,h)<t) $$

### III-B Standard CGMT

Informally, the corollary above has the following interpretation: if $\phi(g,h)$ concentrates to a value $c$ , then $\Phi(G,\gamma)<c+\epsilon$ holds with high probability for $\epsilon>0$ . While the above corollary is sufficient for some applications, it has two distinct drawbacks. Firstly, it only provides a probabilistic upper bound, without a corresponding lower bound the exact value of $\Phi$ cannot be determined asymptotically. Secondarily, it only provides information about the value of $\Phi$ in terms of the optimal value of $\phi$ but provides no information about the relationship between their solutions.

It turns out that the inequality from the Corollary 1 can be reversed under the additional assumptions that $\psi(w,v)$ is convex-concave and that the sets ${\cal S}_{w}$ and ${\cal S}_{v}$ are convex. Furthermore, in this case, if the solution of $\phi$ belongs to an open set $\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{S}_{w}$ with high probability then so does the solution of $\Phi$ . Formally, the following theorem holds (see (Thrampoulidis et al.,, 2014; Thrampoulidis et al.,, 2015; Thrampoulidis,, 2016)):

#### Theorem 3 (Convex Gaussian Min-Max Theorem).

Let $\mathcal{S}_{w}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{S}_{v}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be compact convex sets and $\psi(w,v):\mathcal{S}_{w}\times\mathcal{S}_{v}\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex-concave. Furthermore, let $G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , $g\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $h\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ all have i.i.d $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ components. Define

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(G):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}v^{T}Gw+\psi(w,v) \displaystyle\phi(g,h):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\|v\|_{2}g^{T}w+\|w\|_{2}h^{T}v+\psi(w,v) $$

The following statements hold:

- 1. For any $\eta,c\in\mathbb{R}$ $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|\Phi(G)-c|>\eta)\leq 2\mathbb{P}(|\phi(g,h)-c|>\eta)$

- 2. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be an arbitrary open subset of $\mathcal{S}_{w}$ and $\mathcal{S}^{c}=\mathcal{S}_{w}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ . Define: $\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}^{c}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}v^{T}Gw+\psi(w,v)$ $\displaystyle\phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(g,h):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}^{c}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\|v\|_{2}g^{T}w+\|w\|_{2}h^{T}v+\psi(w,v)$ $\displaystyle w_{\Phi}(G):=\argmin_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}v^{T}Gw+\psi(w,v)$ Assume also that there exist $\epsilon>0$ , $\delta>0$ , $\bar{\phi},\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}$ such that • $\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}\geq\bar{\phi}+3\delta$ • $\phi(g,h)<\bar{\phi}+\delta$ with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ • $\phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}>\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta$ with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ Then $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(w_{\Phi}(G)\in\mathcal{S})\geq 1-4\epsilon$

### III-C Multi-source Gaussian regression

To demonstrate the power of the novel CGMT presented in this work, we will focus on two examples. Here we consider Multi-source Gaussian Regression. Consider a setup of $k$ -measurement devices and consider a dataset of $\left\{(x_{i}^{l},y_{i}^{l})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}\right\}_{i=1,l=1}^{n,k}$ of $n$ $d-$ dimensional observations by each of the $k$ devices, with corresponding labels $y_{i}^{l}$ . We will define $y_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ element-wise by $(y_{l})_{i}=y_{i,l}$ and similarly define $X_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ by means of $(X_{l})_{i,j}=(x^{l}_{i})_{j}$ . Our regression problem then takes the form of

$$ \min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{nk}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell_{l}\left(y_{l}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}X_{l}\theta\right)+R(\theta), $$

where $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\ell_{l}$ and $R$ are convex loss and regularization functions respectively. We shall assume that $X_{l}$ are independent Gaussian matrices, defined by $X_{l}=G_{l}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}$ , where $G_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ have i.i.d standard Gaussian elements, and $\Sigma_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ are covariance matrices. Finally, we will assume the following model, which relates the labels to the datapoints:

$$ y_{l}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}X_{l}\theta^{*}+\nu_{l}, $$

where $\theta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denotes the "true" relationship, and $\nu_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is i.i.d zero mean noise, with variance $\sigma_{\nu,l}^{2}$ independent of $X_{l}$ . In other words, we assume some true linear relationship, between data and labels subject to corruption due to noise. We allow for different noise power for each channel. We will specifically concentrate on the generalization error of this regression problem, which we will define by:

$$ \mathcal{E}_{gen}=\frac{1}{2k}\mathbb{E}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\left\|y_{l,new}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}x_{l,new}^{T}\hat{\theta}\right\|^{2} $$

where $x_{l,new}$ are drawn from the same distribution as $X_{l}$ and $y_{l,new}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}x_{l,new}^{T}\theta^{*}+\nu_{l,new}$ , where $\nu_{l,new}$ is new noise drawn from the same noise distribution. We discuss and analyze this multi-source regression problem in section V-A.

One cannot leverage the usual CGMT to tackle the problem in (2) which will be made explicit in the following. By setting $z_{l}:=y_{l}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}X_{l}\theta$ and introducing Lagrange multipliers:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\theta,z_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\max_{v_{l}}R(\theta)+\frac{1}{nk}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}v_{l}^{T}X_{l}\theta-v_{l}^{T}y_{l}+v_{l}^{T}z_{l}+\ell_{l}(z_{l})\right] $$

Defining $X^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{T}|X_{2}^{T}|\ldots|X_{k}^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ and $v^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}v_{1}^{T}&v_{2}^{T}&\ldots v_{k}^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ allows us to rewrite (4) as

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\theta,z_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\max_{v}R(\theta)+\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}v^{T}X\theta+\frac{1}{nk}v^{T}z-\frac{1}{nk}v^{T}y+\frac{1}{nk}\ell(z), $$

where $z^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}z_{1}^{T}\ldots z_{k}^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ , $y^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}y_{1}^{T}\ldots y_{k}^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ , and $\ell(z)=\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell_{l}(z_{l})$ . Now note that we cannot apply the standard CGMT to either of (4) or (5) since in (4) the vector $\theta$ couples the optimizations over $v_{l},z_{l}$ , and in (5), as discussed, the rows of the Gaussian matrix $X$ are not identically distributed. We therefore need a new CGMT that can apply to the Gaussian process, $v^{T}X\theta=\sum_{l=1}^{k}v_{l}G_{l}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}\theta$ , which is the main contribution of the current paper.

### III-D Binary classification for Gaussian Mixture Models

We next consider the binary linear classification problem on data generated from a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with arbitrary covariance. To be precise, the data $\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is generated as:

$$ \mathbf{x}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k})\quad\text{where}\quad k\sim\textit{Unif}\{1,2\}, $$

$\mu_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are the mean vectors and $\Sigma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ are the corresponding covariance matrices. For simplicity, we assume that we uniformly sample from both the mixtures but the analysis can be extended to arbitrary sampling priors. We set the labels $y_{i}=1$ if data is generated from the cluster with mean $\mu_{1}$ and $y_{i}=-1$ if data is generated from the cluster with mean $\mu_{2}$ . We then formulate the learning objective in terms of the following regression problem.

$$ \min_{w}\mathcal{L}((A+M)w-z)+\lambda f(w) $$

where $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ controls the degree of regularization, $M^{T}=(\underbrace{\begin{matrix}\mu_{1}&...&\mu_{1}\end{matrix}}_{\frac{n}{2}}\underbrace{\begin{matrix}\mu_{2}&...&\mu_{2}\end{matrix}}_{\frac{n}{2}})$ encodes the means corresponding to each class, $z^{T}=(\underbrace{\begin{matrix}1&...&1\end{matrix}}_{\frac{n}{2}}\underbrace{\begin{matrix}-1&...&-1\end{matrix}}_{\frac{n}{2}})$ corresponds to the labels and

$$ A=\begin{pmatrix}G_{1}&0\\
0&G_{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
\Sigma_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
\end{pmatrix} $$

where $G_{1},G_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{n}{2}\times d}$ are Gaussian matrices with iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ entries. Therefore, the rows of $A+M$ denote the data generated by the GMM and without loss of generality we assume that the data is ordered and split into two equal halves from the two mixtures. Additionally, we assume both loss function $\mathcal{L}(\cdot)$ and regularization function $f(\cdot)$ to be separable convex functions. Given a linear $\hat{w}$ , the classification rule at inference is $\hat{y}(x)=\text{sign}(\hat{w}^{T}x)$ . The classification error, or the error on unseen data, generated for the above GMM is given as:

$$ E(\hat{w})=\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{\mu_{1}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{1}\hat{w}}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}Q\left(-\frac{\mu_{2}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{2}\hat{w}}}\right) $$

where $Q(\cdot)$ is the standard Gaussian CCDF.

Finally, to make the results as explicit as possible we assume that $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$ are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and their matching entries are correlated according to $\mathbb{E}\mu_{1i}\mu_{2i}=r$ for some $-1\leq r\leq 1$ . Under this assumption we have $\|\mu_{1}\|\approx\|\mu_{2}\|\approx\sqrt{d}$ and $\mu_{1}^{T}\mu_{2}\approx rd$ .** * Theorem 6 further below is true for arbitrary $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$ and one can still use it to derive versions of Theorem 7 and Corollary 2 for any other given model for $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$ but we prefer to follow with this specific assumption because it is meant to capture the simplest case of two ”typical” $d$ -dimensional vectors that are not necessarily orthogonal.

To illustrate why one cannot just readily apply the standard CGMT in this setting, we have to spell out (6) further. The standard way of dealing with (6) is introducing $u:=(A+M)w-z$ and inserting a Lagrange multiplier, after which we would have:

$$ \min_{w,u}\max_{v}v^{T}Aw+v^{T}Mw-v^{T}z-v^{T}u+\mathcal{L}(u)+\lambda f(w) $$

The standard CGMT cannot be applied here because $A$ is not i.i.d. To try resolving it, one can denote $v^{T}=(v_{1}^{T},v_{2}^{T})$ for $v_{1},v_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{n}{2}}$ and obtain

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w,u}\max_{v_{1},v_{2}}v_{1}^{T}G_{1}\Sigma_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+v_{2}^{T}G_{2}\Sigma_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+v^{T}Mw-v^{T}z-v^{T}u+\mathcal{L}(u)+\lambda f(w) $$

Note first of all that the objective above does not separate into a CGMT instance with $G_{1}$ and a CGMT instance with $G_{2}$ because $w$ "sees" both of these matrices. If $\Sigma_{1}=\Sigma_{2}$ , we can define $\tilde{w}=\Sigma_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}w$ , $(M\Sigma_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}})^{T}=\left(\tilde{M}_{1}|\tilde{M}_{2}\right)^{T},\tilde{M}_{1},\tilde{M}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\frac{n}{2}}$ , $\tilde{f}(x)=f(\Sigma_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}x)$ and arrive at:

$$ \min_{\tilde{w},u}\max_{v}v^{T}(G_{1}^{T}|G_{2}^{T})^{T}\tilde{w}+v^{T}\tilde{M}^{T}\tilde{w}-v^{T}z-v^{T}u+\mathcal{L}(u)+\lambda\tilde{f}(\tilde{w}) $$

Hence, when $\Sigma_{1}=\Sigma_{2}$ , since $(G_{1}^{T}|G_{2}^{T})$ is i.i.d. Gaussian we can analyze (8) using the standard CGMT. However, for the case of general $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ the same argument does not apply and it appears that one just has to develop a framework allowing for terms of the form $v_{1}^{T}G_{1}\Sigma_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+v_{2}^{T}G_{2}\Sigma_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}w$ to be present in the objective. This is essentially what Theorem 4 addresses.

## IV Main results

We will occasionally shorten $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ to $\|\cdot\|$ for brevity in the expressions below.

#### Lemma 1.

Let $G_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times d},\dots,G_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times d}$ , $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}$ , $g_{1},\dots,g_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $h_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,h_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ all have i.i.d $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ components, $\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\beta_{1}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,\beta_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ be arbitrary functions, $I,J_{1},\dots,J_{k}$ be finite sets and $\{w_{i}\}_{i\in I}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $\{u_{j_{1}}\}_{j_{1}\in J_{1}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,\{u_{j_{k}}\}_{j_{k}\in J_{k}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ be arbitrary discrete subsets. Then the following two Gaussian Processes defined on $I\times J$ , where $J=J_{1}\times\dots\times J_{k}$ and $j\in J$ denotes $(j_{1},\dots,j_{k})\in J_{1}\times\dots\times J_{k}$ , satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 1:

$$ \displaystyle Y_{ij}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\left[\beta_{\ell}(v_{j\ell})^{T}G_{\ell}\alpha_{\ell}(w_{i})+\gamma_{\ell}\|\alpha_{\ell}(w_{i})\|\|\beta_{\ell}(v_{j\ell})\|\right] \displaystyle X_{ij}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\left[\|\beta_{\ell}(v_{j\ell})\|\alpha_{\ell}(w_{i})^{T}g_{\ell}+\|\alpha_{\ell}(w_{i})\|h_{\ell}^{T}\beta_{\ell}(v_{j\ell})\right] $$

Moreover, the processes defined by $\tilde{X}_{ji}=X_{ij}$ and $\tilde{Y}_{ji}=Y_{ij}$ on $J\times I$ satisfy these assumptions as well.

Consider arbitrary convex functions $\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\beta_{1}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,\beta_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ , and define:

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(G):= \displaystyle\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\beta_{\ell}(v_{\ell})^{T}G_{\ell}\alpha_{\ell}(w)+\psi(w,v) \displaystyle\phi(g,h):= \displaystyle\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\left[\|\beta_{\ell}(v_{\ell})\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\alpha_{\ell}(w)+\|\alpha_{\ell}(w)\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}\right]+\psi(w,v) $$

After making several additional technical steps, Lemma 1 combined with Theorem 1 can be used to deduce the following generalization of Theorem 3:

#### Theorem 4 (Generalized CGMT).

Let $\mathcal{S}_{w}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{S}_{v_{1}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,\mathcal{S}_{v_{k}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ be compact convex sets. Denote $\mathcal{S}_{v}:=\mathcal{S}_{v_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathcal{S}_{v_{k}}$ , let $v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}$ stand for $(v_{1},\dots,v_{k})\in\mathcal{S}_{v_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathcal{S}_{v_{k}}$ and $\psi(w,v):\mathcal{S}_{w}\times\mathcal{S}_{v}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous, $\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\beta_{1}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,\beta_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ be also arbitrary continuous functions. Furthermore, let $G_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times d},\dots,G_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times d}$ , $g_{1},\dots,g_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $h_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}},\dots,h_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ all have i.i.d $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ components and $G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k})$ , $g=\left(g_{1},\dots,g_{k}\right)$ , $h=\left(h_{1},\dots,h_{k}\right)$ be the corresponding $k$ -tuples. Define $\Phi(G)$ and $\phi(g,h)$ as in (9). Then the following statements hold:

- 1. For any $t\in\mathbb{R}$ we have $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi(G,\gamma)<t)\leq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\phi(g,h)<t)$

- 2. Assume, moreover, that $\psi$ is convex-concave and $\alpha_{\ell}$ , $\beta_{\ell}$ are affine functions of their inputs, that is they take the form of $\alpha_{\ell}(w)=A_{\ell}w+a_{\ell},\beta_{\ell}(u)=B_{\ell}u+b_{\ell}$ for some $A_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},B_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}},a_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},b_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}}$ . Then for all $\eta,c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\eta>0$ the following statement holds:

$$ \mathbb{P}(|\Phi(G)-c|>\eta)\leq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(|\phi(g,h)-c|>\eta) $$

- 3. Assume the same setting as in (2). Let $\mathcal{S}$ be an arbitrary open subset of $\mathcal{S}_{w}$ and $\mathcal{S}^{c}=\mathcal{S}_{w}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ . Define: $\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}^{c}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\beta_{\ell}(v_{\ell})^{T}G_{\ell}\alpha_{\ell}(w)+\psi(w,v)$ $\displaystyle\phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(g,h):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}^{c}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\left[\|\beta_{\ell}(v_{\ell})\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\alpha_{\ell}(w)+\|\alpha_{\ell}(w)\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}\right]+\psi(w,v)$ $\displaystyle w_{\Phi}(G):=\argmin_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\beta_{\ell}(v_{\ell})^{T}G_{\ell}\alpha_{\ell}(w)+\psi(w,v)$ Assume also that there exist $\epsilon,\delta>0$ , $\bar{\phi},\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}$ such that • $\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}\geq\bar{\phi}+3\delta$ • $\phi(g,h)<\bar{\phi}+\delta$ with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ • $\phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}>\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta$ with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ Then $\mathbb{P}(w_{\Phi}(G)\in\mathcal{S})\geq 1-2^{k+1}\epsilon$

Part 2 of Theorem 4 says that if $\phi(g,h)$ concentrates to a value $c$ , then so does $\Phi(G)$ , albeit with a possibly slightly worse tail bound. Moreover, it turns out that $\phi(g,h)$ concentrates to $\mathbb{E}\phi(g,h)$ exponentially fast, which we prove in Appendix B. As such, Theorem 4 implies that $\Phi(G)$ concentrates exponentially fast to the same value. Part $3$ of the theorem says that if the solution of $\phi(g,h)$ satisfies a certain property with probability very close to $1$ , such as for example belonging to a ball of a fixed radius, then the same is true for the solution of $\Phi(G)$ .

#### Remark 1.

We would also like to point out Theorem 3 from Dhifallah and Lu, (2021) that considers similar objectives, namely ones of the following form, where the entries of $G_{\ell}$ are again i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ :

$$ \Phi(G):=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}v_{\ell}^{T}G_{\ell}w_{\ell}+\psi(w,v) $$

After establishing the corresponding comparison inequality, Dhifallah and Lu, (2021) proceed to apply it to study the effects of noise injection on the generalization performance of Random Feature Models. Our work is concerned with characterizing the generalization performance for binary classification with arbitrary covariance matrices and multi-source Gaussian regression. These problems lead to analyzing objectives of the following form:

$$ \Phi(G)=\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}v_{\ell}^{T}G_{\ell}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\psi(w,v) $$

Note that (11) differs from (10) in two substantial ways. First, (11) explicitly contains the covariance matrices, which is clearly crucial for the applications we mentioned. Second, note that in (11) the same $w$ is shared between each term, while in (10) each $w_{\ell}$ is taken to be different. If, however, one were to still take each $w_{\ell}$ to be the same in (10), analyzing the resulting problem would reduce to the standard CGMT with a larger Gaussian matrix $G=[G_{1},\dots,G_{k}]^{T}$ .

#### Remark 2.

The first arxiv version of the present manuscript considered only the less general case of $A_{\ell}=\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ being an arbitrary PSD matrix, $B_{\ell}=I_{n_{k}}$ , $a_{\ell}=0$ and $b_{\ell}=0$ as this was enough to address the applications mentioned in Subsections III-C and III-D . Concurrent to the posting of this paper on arxiv, the authors noticed the posting of Jain et al., (2024) which considers a different pair of processes to which CGMT can be applied. Inspired by combining this work and theirs, we note that our main Theorem 4 can be generalized even further. In terms of the terminology above, the processes designed in Jain et al., (2024) correspond to $A_{\ell}=I_{d}$ and $B_{\ell}=I_{n_{\ell}}$ and arbitrary $a_{\ell},b_{\ell}$ .

## V Applications

### V-A Multi-source regression

We recall the problem given in equation (2). Also recall the definition of the Moreau envelope, for a function $f$ and matrix $T$ :

$$ \mathcal{M}_{T\ f(\cdot)}(x)=\min_{z}f(z)+\frac{1}{2}(x-z)^{T}T^{-1}(x-z), $$

where $T^{-1}$ is a positive definite matrix. We also note that the optimal point of the optimization in (12) is the proximal operator, denoted $\mathrm{prox}_{T\ f(\cdot)}(x)$ . The application of the generalized CGMT to the multi-source regression problem gives us the following theorem:

#### Theorem 5 (Multi-source Generalization Error).

Consider the following scalarized optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\xi,q\succeq 0}\max_{\beta,r\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}+\frac{1}{nk}\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}I\ \ell_{l}}\left(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}\right) \displaystyle-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{d}\mathcal{M}_{A^{-1}\ R}\left(\theta^{*}-A^{-1}b\right) $$

Here $\xi,q,\beta,r\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ are element-wise non-negative, and $h_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ for $l=1,\ldots,k$ are i.i.d standard Gaussian vectors independent of each other. Furthermore, $A$ and $b$ are defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle A(r,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}=\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{k}}\Sigma_{l}\right) \displaystyle b(\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}=\left(\frac{1}{k}\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\beta_{l}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}g_{l}\right). $$

We denote by $\hat{r}_{i},\hat{\xi}_{i},\hat{\beta}_{i},\hat{q}_{i}$ the optimal values of the scalarized optimization problem, and define $\hat{A}=A(\hat{r},\hat{\xi})$ and $\hat{b}=b(\hat{\beta})$ . Then the generalization error (as defined in equation 3) for the multi-source Gaussian Regression problem is given by:

$$ \mathcal{E}_{gen}=\frac{1}{2k}\mathbb{E}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\left\|y_{l,new}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}x_{l,new}^{T}\mathrm{prox}_{\hat{A}^{-1}\ R}(\theta^{*}-\hat{A}^{-1}\hat{b})\right\| $$

### V-B Binary classification for general GMMs

In this section, we provide the precise asymptotic analysis of binary linear classification for data generated from a GMM with arbitrary covariances.

#### Theorem 6 (Binary Classification Error).

The classification error obtained from the solution of (6) is given as

$$ \frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{\gamma_{1}}{\theta_{1}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}Q\left(-\frac{\gamma_{2}}{\theta_{2}}\right) $$

where $\gamma_{i}$ and $\theta_{i}$ are solutions of the following scalar optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\tau_{i},\theta_{i},\zeta_{i}\geq 0,\gamma_{i}}\max_{\beta_{i}\geq 0,\eta_{i}}\lambda\mathcal{M}_{\lambda\ f(\Sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}})}\left(\Sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}x\right)-\frac{x^{T}\Sigma^{-1}x}{2} \displaystyle+\sum^{2}_{i=1}\left[\beta_{i}\frac{\tau_{i}}{2}+\mathcal{M}_{\frac{\tau_{i}}{\beta_{i}}\ \mathcal{L}}\left(\gamma_{i}\mathds{1}-\theta_{i}h_{i}-z_{i}\right)-\frac{\theta_{i}\zeta_{i}}{2}-\eta_{i}\gamma_{i}\right] $$

where $\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^{2}\frac{\zeta_{i}}{\theta_{i}}\Sigma_{i}$ and $x=\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma_{i}^{\frac{1}{2}}g_{i}-\eta_{i}\mu_{i}$

In the special case of the $\ell_{2}$ -norm square loss and regularization, we have the following simplified result:

#### Theorem 7.

The classification error obtained from the solution of (6) when $\mathcal{L}(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|^{2}$ and $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|^{2}$ is given as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{\gamma_{1}+2}{\sqrt{\frac{8}{n}\tau_{1}^{2}-\gamma_{1}^{2}}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{-\gamma_{2}+2}{\sqrt{\frac{8}{n}\tau_{2}^{2}-\gamma_{2}^{2}}}\right) $$

where $\beta_{i},\gamma_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}$ are solutions of the following scalar optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\tau_{i}\geq 0}\max_{\beta_{i}\geq 0,\gamma_{i}}-\frac{1}{4}\text{Tr}\Bigl[(\lambda I+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\Sigma_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\Sigma_{2})^{-1}(\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}rI+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\Sigma_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}I)\Bigr] \displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}\tau_{i}}{2}-\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}}-\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}(-1)^{i+1}}{4\tau_{i}}-\frac{\beta_{i}^{2}}{4}\right] $$

The performances of various classification algorithms have been analyzed in depth using the standard CGMT for the case of scalar $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ (see, for example, (Mignacco et al.,, 2020; Thrampoulidis et al.,, 2020; Akhtiamov et al.,, 2023)). As a baby step towards developing a better understanding of the effects of the structure of $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ on the classification error, we apply Theorem 7 to the following explicitly defined model:

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{1}=\sigma_{1}^{2}I+\nu_{1}\nu_{1}^{T}~~~\mbox{and}~~~\Sigma_{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}I+\nu_{2}\nu_{2}^{T} \displaystyle\text{ where }\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma\in\mathbb{R}~~~\mbox{and}~~~\nu_{1},\nu_{2}\text{ are i.i.d. }\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) $$

Plugging in these assumptions into Theorem 7 yields the following Corollary.

#### Corollary 2.

The classification error obtained from the solution of (6) when $\mathcal{L}(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|^{2},f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|^{2}$ for $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ defined as above is given as:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{\gamma_{1}+2}{\sqrt{\frac{8}{n}\tau_{1}^{2}-\gamma_{1}^{2}}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{-\gamma_{2}+2}{\sqrt{\frac{8}{n}\tau_{2}^{2}-\gamma_{2}^{2}}}\right) $$

where $\beta_{i},\gamma_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}$ are solutions of the following scalar optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\tau_{i}\geq 0}\max_{\beta_{i}\geq 0,\gamma_{i}}(d-2)(\lambda+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\sigma^{2}_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\sigma^{2}_{2})^{-1}\left(\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}r+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[\beta_{i}^{2}\sigma^{2}_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}\right]\right) \displaystyle+(\lambda+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}(\sigma^{2}_{1}+\sigma^{2}d)+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\sigma^{2}_{2})^{-1}\left(\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}r+\beta_{1}^{2}\sigma^{2}d+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[\beta_{i}^{2}\sigma^{2}_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}\right]\right) \displaystyle+(\lambda+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\sigma^{2}_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}(\sigma^{2}_{2}+\sigma^{2}d))^{-1}\left(\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}r+\beta_{2}^{2}\sigma^{2}d+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[\beta_{i}^{2}\sigma^{2}_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}\right]\right) \displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}\tau_{i}}{2}-\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}}-\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}(-1)^{i+1}}{4\tau_{i}}-\frac{\beta_{i}^{2}}{4}\right] $$

#### Remark 3.

Since the first term in the objective above has $(d-2)$ in front of it, and the other two do not, one might approximate the objective by only the first term for large enough $d$ . Indeed, even though the second and the third terms have some occurrences of $d$ as well, in both cases this quantity is present both in the numerator and the denominator of a certain fraction. This tells us that as $d$ grows large, we should not expect the performance to be very different from the case $\tilde{\Sigma}_{1}=\sigma_{1}^{2}I,\tilde{\Sigma}_{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}I$ , as this is what the first term corresponds to if we replace $(d-2)$ by $d$ , again by the virtue of the fact that $d$ is large. Since this observation is not rigorous, we check it numerically in the next section.

To conclude, note that it is also feasible to study linear classification for GMMs via approaches based on AMP (see (Loureiro et al.,, 2021)). Since the present paper is devoted to studying approaches based on Gaussian comparison inequalities, covering other methods goes beyond its scope. But in any case, the authors believe that developing new tools for tackling a problem is always of value, as it usually leads to new insights, such as Remark 3, which has not been observed before in the literature to the best of the authors’ knowledge.

## VII Conclusion and future work

We presented a new pair of Gaussian processes that satisfy Gordon’s comparison conditions and thereby developed a generalization of the Convex Gaussian Min-Max Theorem. We further demonstrated its use in two examples, namely multi-source regression and binary classification for Gaussian data with arbitrary covariance matrices. Future work would be to see if further pairs of comparable processes can be found. Of particular interest are those where $G_{\ell}$ and $G_{\ell^{\prime}}$ do not have to be independent for $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ .
