$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(-\phi(g,h)<-c-\eta)=\mathbb{P}\left(-\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}+\psi(w,v)<-c-\eta\right)= \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\min_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}(-g_{\ell})^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}(-h_{\ell})^{T}v_{\ell}-\psi(w,v)<-c-\eta\right)= \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\min_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}-\psi(w,v)<-c-\eta\right)\leq \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\min_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\max_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}-\psi(w,v)<-c-\eta\right)=\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\phi}(g,h)<-c-\eta) \displaystyle\text{ where }\tilde{\phi}(g,h)=\min_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\max_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\|v_{\ell}\|_{2}g_{\ell}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w+\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{2}h_{\ell}^{T}v_{\ell}-\psi(w,v) $$

Denoting $C=c-\eta$ and $\tilde{C}=-c-\eta$ , we then have to show the following two inequalities:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi(G)<C)\leq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\phi(g,h)<C) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\Phi}(G)<\tilde{C})\leq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\phi}(g,h)<\tilde{C}) $$

Note that according to Lemma 2, it is enough to prove the desired inequalities for any sequence of $\delta$ -nets $\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{w},\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v}$ with $\delta\to 0$ . Indeed, we would then have

$$ \mathbb{P}(\Phi(G)>C)\geq\mathbb{P}(\Phi^{\delta}(G)>C)\geq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\phi^{\delta}(g,h)>C)\geq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\phi(g,h)>C) $$

as well as the same chain of inequalities for $\tilde{\Phi}(G),\tilde{\phi}(g,h)$ and $\tilde{C}$ . Moreover, we can assume that each $\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v}$ is of the form $\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v}=\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v_{k}}$ . Denote $\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{w}=\{w_{i}\}_{i\in I},\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v_{1}}=\{u_{j_{1}}\}_{j_{1}\in J_{1}},\dots,\mathcal{S}^{\delta}_{v_{k}}=\{u_{j_{k}}\}_{j_{k}\in J_{k}}$ , $t_{ij}=C-\psi(w_{i},v_{j}),\tilde{t}_{ji}=\tilde{C}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})$ . Construct processes $X_{ij},\tilde{X}_{ji},Y_{ij},\tilde{Y}_{ji}$ as in the statement of Lemma 1 for $I,J_{1},\dots,J_{k}$ introduced in the previous sentence. Applying Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 to $X,Y,t$ and $\tilde{X},\tilde{Y},\tilde{t}$ we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[Y_{ij}\geq t_{ij}])\geq\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[X_{ij}\geq t_{ij}]) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{j\in J}\bigcup_{i\in I}[\tilde{Y}_{ji}\geq\tilde{t}_{ji}])\geq\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{j\in J}\bigcup_{i\in I}[\tilde{X}_{ji}\geq\tilde{t}_{ji}]) $$

We then deduce:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\min_{i\in I}\max_{j\in J}{X_{ij}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<C})=1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[X_{ij}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})\geq C])=1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[X_{ij}\geq t_{ij}])\geq \displaystyle\geq 1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[Y_{ij}\geq t_{ij}])=1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigcup_{j\in J}[Y_{ij}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})\geq C])=\mathbb{P}(\min_{i\in I}\max_{j\in J}{Y_{ij}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<C}) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\min_{j\in J}\max_{i\in I}{\tilde{X}_{ji}-\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<\tilde{C}})=1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{j\in J}\bigcup_{i\in I}[\tilde{X}_{ji}-\psi(w_{i},v_{j})\geq\tilde{C}])=1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{j\in J}\bigcup_{i\in I}[\tilde{X}_{ji}\geq\tilde{t}_{ji}])\geq \displaystyle\geq 1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{j\in J}\bigcup_{i\in I}[\tilde{Y}_{ji}\geq\tilde{t}_{ji}])=1-\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{j\in J}\bigcup_{i\in I}[\tilde{Y}_{ji}-\psi(w_{i},v_{j})\geq\tilde{C}])=\mathbb{P}(\min_{j\in J}\max_{i\in I}{\tilde{Y}_{ji}-\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<\tilde{C}}) $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\min_{i\in I}\max_{j\in J}{X_{ij}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<C})=\mathbb{P}(\phi^{\delta}(g,h)<C) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\min_{j\in J}\max_{i\in I}{\tilde{X}_{ji}-\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<\tilde{C}})=\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\phi}^{\delta}(g,h)<\tilde{C}) $$

Hence, it suffices to show the following two inequalities:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi^{\delta}(G)<C)\geq\frac{1}{2^{k}}\mathbb{P}(\min_{i\in I}\max_{j\in J}{Y_{ij}+\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<C}) \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\Phi}^{\delta}(G)<\tilde{C})\geq\frac{1}{2^{k}}\mathbb{P}(\min_{j\in J}\max_{i\in I}{\tilde{Y}_{ji}-\psi(w_{i},v_{j})<\tilde{C}}) $$

The latter inequalities follow directly by conditioning on the event $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{k}>0$ , which happens with probability $\frac{1}{2^{k}}$ .

2. As we know from the proof of the previous part of the theorem, the following upper bound takes place:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi(G)<\bar{\phi}+\delta)\leq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\phi<\bar{\phi}+\delta)\leq 2^{k}\epsilon $$

Since $\mathcal{S}^{c}$ is compact, we can apply the same $\delta$ -net argument to deduce the following inequality as well:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G)<\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta)\leq 2^{k}\mathbb{P}(\phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}<\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta)\leq 2^{k}\epsilon $$

Combining the results above implies:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\{\Phi(G)>\bar{\phi}+\delta\}\cup\{\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G)<\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta\})\leq 2^{k+1}\epsilon $$

Which yields:

$$ \displaystyle 1-2^{k+1}\epsilon<\mathbb{P}(\{\Phi(G)\leq\bar{\phi}+\delta\}\cap\{\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G)\geq\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta\}) $$

By assumption $\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}>\bar{\phi}+3\delta$ . Thus:

$$ \displaystyle 1-2^{k+1}\epsilon<\mathbb{P}(\{\Phi(G)\leq\bar{\phi}+\delta\}\cap\{\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G)\geq\bar{\phi}_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}-\delta\})\leq\mathbb{P}(\Phi(G)<\Phi_{\mathcal{S}^{c}}(G)-\delta) $$

Therefore:

$$ \displaystyle 1-2^{k+1}\epsilon<\mathbb{P}(w_{\Phi(G)}\in\mathcal{S}) $$

∎

We proceed to prove Lemma 1 now:

#### Proof.

Recall the definitions of the Gaussian processes we have to compare, where $v_{j}$ stands as a shorthand notation for $(v_{j_{1}},\dots,v_{j_{k}})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}$ :

$$ Y_{ij}={v_{j}}^{T}\begin{pmatrix}G_{1}&0&\cdots&0\\
0&G_{2}&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\cdots&G_{k}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
\Sigma_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
\vdots\\
\Sigma_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{pmatrix}w_{i}+\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\gamma_{\ell}\|v_{j_{\ell}}\|\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i}\|~~~\mbox{and}~~~X_{ij}=\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{j_{\ell}}\|w_{i}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}g_{\ell}+{v_{j_{\ell}}}^{T}h_{\ell}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{i}\| $$

Calculating the covariances is straightforward using that $G_{\ell}$ and $G_{\ell^{\prime}}$ are independent whenever $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ :

$$ \mathbb{E}[Y_{ij}Y_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}]=\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}{v_{j_{\ell}}}^{T}v_{j^{\prime}_{\ell}}w_{i}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}w_{i^{\prime}}+\|v_{j_{\ell}}\|\|v_{j^{\prime}_{\ell}}\|\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i}\|\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i^{\prime}}\| $$

$$ \mathbb{E}[X_{ij}X_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}]=\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{j_{\ell}}\|\|v_{j^{\prime}_{\ell}}\|w_{i}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}w_{i^{\prime}}+{v_{j_{\ell}}}^{T}v_{j^{\prime}_{\ell}}\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i}\|\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i^{\prime}}\| $$

Hence, the third assumption of Gordon’s Gaussian comparison theorem follows from Cauchy-Schwartz:

$$ \mathbb{E}[Y_{ij}Y_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}-X_{ij}X_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}]=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}({v_{j_{\ell}}}^{T}v_{j^{\prime}_{\ell}}-\|v_{j_{\ell}}\|\|v_{j^{\prime}_{\ell}}\|)({w_{i}}^{T}\Sigma_{\ell}w_{i^{\prime}}-\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i}\|\|\Sigma_{\ell}^{\frac{1}{2}}w_{i^{\prime}}\|)\geq 0 $$

Moreover, if either $i=i^{\prime}$ or $j=j^{\prime}$ then the expression above vanishes, implying the first and the second assumptions as well. The proof is almost identical for the processes $\tilde{X}$ and $\tilde{Y}$ .

∎

## X Concentration

#### Lemma 3.

$\phi(g,h)$ is a $\sigma\sqrt{2}R_{w}R_{v}$ - Lipschitz function of $(g,h)$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\sigma=\max_{\ell}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}\|_{op} \displaystyle R_{w}=\max_{w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}}\{\|w\|\} \displaystyle R_{v}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{v}}\{\|v\|\} $$

#### Proof.

Let $g_{1},g_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\ell}$ and $h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\ell}$ be $\ell$ -tuples of i.i.d. Gaussian vectors.

Define:

$$ \displaystyle(w_{1},v_{1})=\argmin_{w\in S_{w}}\max_{v\in S_{v}}\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{\ell}\|w^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}{g_{1}}_{\ell}+v_{\ell}^{T}{h_{1}}_{\ell}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w\|+\psi(w,v) \displaystyle v_{2}=\argmax_{v\in S_{v}}\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{\ell}\|w_{1}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}g_{2\ell}+v_{\ell}^{T}h_{2\ell}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{1}\|+\psi(w_{1},v) $$

We then have:

$$ \displaystyle\phi(g_{2},h_{2})\leq\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{2}\|w_{1}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}{g_{2}}_{\ell}+{v_{2}}_{\ell}^{T}{h_{2}}_{\ell}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{1}\|+\psi(w_{1},v_{2}) \displaystyle\phi(g_{1},h_{1})\geq\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{2}\|w_{1}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}{g_{1}}_{\ell}+{v_{2}}_{\ell}^{T}{h_{1}}_{\ell}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{1}\|+\psi(w_{1},v_{2}) $$

Therefore:

$$ \displaystyle\phi(g_{2},h_{2})-\phi(g_{1},h_{1}) \displaystyle\leq\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{2}\|w_{1}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}(g_{2\ell}-g_{1\ell})+{v_{2}}_{\ell}^{T}(h_{2\ell}-h_{1\ell})\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{1}\|\leq \displaystyle\leq\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{2}\|\|w_{1}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}\|\|g_{1\ell}-g_{2\ell}\|+\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{1}\|\|v_{2}\|\|h_{1\ell}-h_{2\ell}\|= \displaystyle=\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{2}\|\|w_{1}^{T}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}\|(\|g_{1\ell}-g_{2\ell}\|+\|h_{1\ell}-h_{2\ell}\|)\leq $$

$$ \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|v_{2}\|^{2}\|\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\ell}w_{1}\|^{2}}\sqrt{\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|g_{1\ell}-g_{2\ell}\|^{2}+\|h_{1\ell}-h_{2\ell}\|^{2}}\leq \displaystyle\leq\sigma\sqrt{2}R_{w}R_{v}\sqrt{\sum^{k}_{\ell=1}\|g_{1\ell}-g_{2\ell}\|^{2}+\|h_{1\ell}-h_{2\ell}\|^{2}} $$

∎

#### Corollary 3.

Under the notation from the lemma above,

$$ \mathbb{P}(|\phi(g,h)-\mathbb{E}\phi(g,h)|>\epsilon)\leq exp(-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}R^{2}_{w}R^{2}_{v}}) $$

#### Proof.

Follows immediately from the lemma above and Theorem 5.6 in Boucheron et al., (2013). ∎

## XI Applications

### XI-A Multi-Source Gaussian Regression

#### XI-A1 Assumptions

The following assumptions are necessary for the Multi-source Gaussian Regression Results to hold.

- A1 The functions $\ell_{l}$ , for all $l=1,\ldots,k$ and $R$ are proper, lower semi-continuous, and convex. Furthermore, the function $\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell_{l}+R$ should be coercive, by which we mean: $\displaystyle\lim_{\left\|\bm{\theta}\right\|_{2}\rightarrow\infty}\left(\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell_{l}+R\right)(\theta)=+\infty$

- A2 the Regularization function $R$ must satisfy the following scaling condition. For any vector $x$ such that $\left\|x\right\|_{2}\leq c\sqrt{d}$ for some constant $c$ , this implies that $\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\partial R(z)}\left\|z\right\|\leq C\sqrt{d}$ where $\partial R$ is the subdifferential of $R$ , and $C$ is some constant.

- A3 the noise $\nu_{l}$ , for all $l=1,\ldots,k$ , is a zero mean sub-Gaussian random vector, with variance $\sigma_{\bm{\nu},l}$ .

We recall the setup discussed in section III-C

$$ \min_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{nk}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell_{l}\left(y_{l}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}X_{l}\theta\right)+R(\theta), $$

Where $y_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},X_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d},\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . We recall that $X_{l}$ are Gaussian matrices, defined by $G_{k}\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}$ , where $G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ has i.i.d Gaussian elements, and $\Sigma_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ are PSD covariance matrices. Finally, recalling the assumption that $\mathbf{y}_{k}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}X\theta^{*}+\nu_{k}$ where $\bm{\nu}_{k}$ is i.i.d zero mean noise, with variance $\sigma_{\nu,k}$

We first define $e=\theta-\theta^{*}$ as the error vector and rewrite our optimization as

$$ \displaystyle\min_{e\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{nk}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell_{l}(\nu_{l}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}G_{l}\Sigma^{1/2}\mathbf{e})+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

We then let $z_{l}=\nu_{l}-G_{l}\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e$ and let $\lambda_{l}$ be a Lagrange multiplier

$$ \displaystyle\min_{e\in\mathbb{R}^{d},Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}}\max_{\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}(z_{l}-\nu_{l}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}G_{l}\Sigma_{k}^{1/2}e)+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})+R(\mathbf{e}+\theta^{*}). $$

Before we can apply our application of the generalized CGMT we must restrict our optimization to compact and convex sets. We demonstrate this in the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4 (Compact and Convex Sets).

Let $\hat{e}$ , $\hat{Z}$ , $\hat{\Lambda}$ be the optimal solution to (20). There exist positive constants $C_{e},C_{Z},C_{\Lambda}$ such that:

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\|\hat{e}\right\|_{2}\leq C_{e}\sqrt{d}\right)\xrightarrow[d\rightarrow\infty]{P}1 \displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\|\hat{Z}\right\|_{2}\leq C_{Z}\sqrt{n}\right)\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{P}1 \displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\|\hat{\Lambda}\right\|_{2}\leq C_{\Lambda}\sqrt{n}\right)\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{P}1 $$

#### Proof.

We first show that the set of minimizers for $e$ is non-empty and compact. We assume that the sum $f(e)=\sum_{l=1}^{k}\ell(\nu_{l}-m^{-1/2}G_{l}\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e)+R(e+\theta^{*})$ is a coercive, proper, and lower-semi continuous functions. As the function is proper, there exists at least a single value $e_{0}$ such that $f(\mathbf{e}_{0})<\infty$ . Furthermore, by the fact that $f$ is coercive, there exists an $\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}\geq 0$ such that for every $e\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ for which $\left\|e-e_{0}\right\|\geq\epsilon$ implies that $f(e)\geq f(e_{0})$ .

We then define

$$ \displaystyle S=\set{e\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\ \left\|e-e_{0}\right\|_{2}\leq\epsilon}, $$

we can then see that $S\cap\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\neq\emptyset$ is nonempty and compact. As such, there there exists an $\hat{e}\in S$ such that $f(\hat{e})=\inf_{e\in S}f(e)\leq f(e_{0})$ . From this we can conclude that $f(\hat{e})\in\inf_{e\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(e)$ , and that the set of minimizers is bounded.

Having determined that the set of minimizers is a compact set with at least one element, we can conclude that there exists a constant $C_{\mathbf{E}}$ which is independent of the ambient dimension $d$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\hat{e}\right\|_{2}\leq C_{e}\sqrt{d}. $$

We now recall equation (20), and examine the optimality condition:

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\lambda_{l}}:\  \displaystyle\nu_{l}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}G_{l}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}e=z_{l} \displaystyle\nabla_{z_{l}}:\  \displaystyle\lambda_{l}\in\partial\ell_{l}(z_{l})\qquad \displaystyle\nabla_{e}:\  \displaystyle\sum_{l=1}^{k}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}G_{l}^{T}\lambda_{l}\in\left.\partial R(x)\right|_{x=e+\theta^{*}}. $$

From the optimality condition of $\lambda_{k}$ we can see that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|z_{l}\right\|\leq\left\|\nu_{l}\right\|_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\left\|G_{l}\right\|_{2}\left\|\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}\right\|_{2}\left\|e\right\| $$

We note that $\nu_{l}$ is a sub-Gaussian random variable, as such its norm can asymptotically be bounded by a $C\sqrt{n}$ for some constant $C$ . Similarly $\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\left\|G_{l}\right\|$ is bounded in operator norm by a constant asymptotically by standard random matrix theory results (see for example (Papaspiliopoulos,, 2020)[corollary 7.3.3]). By making use of the bound on $\left\|e\right\|$ we can find that each $z_{l}$ is bounded in norm. From this we can see that there exists some constant $C_{Z}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\|\hat{Z}\right\|_{2}\leq C_{Z}\sqrt{n}\right)\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{P}1 $$

Finally, the scaling condition on $R$ implies the existence of a constant $C_{\lambda}$ . ∎

We now define the following sets

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{e}=\set{e\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\ \left\|e\right\|\leq C_{e}\sqrt{d}} \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{Z}=\set{Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}}{\ \left\|Z\right\|\leq C_{Z}\sqrt{n}} \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\Lambda}=\set{\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}}{\ \left\|\Lambda\right\|\leq C_{\Lambda}\sqrt{n}}, $$

and note that our optimization problem can be expressed as:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e},Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z}}\max_{\Lambda\in\mathcal{S}_{\Lambda}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}(z_{l}-\nu_{l}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}G_{l}\Sigma_{k}^{1/2}e)+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})+R(e+\theta^{*}) \displaystyle\overset{def}{=}\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}\mathcal{P}(e,G_{1},\cdots,G_{k}) $$

We note that we now have a min-max optimization over compact and convex sets in the form required for the application of theorem 4. We apply the generalized CGMT to $\mathcal{P}$ , from which we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}\left[\min_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z}}\max_{\Lambda\in\mathcal{S}_{\Lambda}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}\left\|\lambda_{l}\right\|g_{l}^{T}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}e+\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}\left\|\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e\right\|h_{l}^{T}\lambda_{l}\right. \displaystyle\left.+\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}z_{l}-\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}\nu_{l}+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})+R(e+\theta^{*})\right] \displaystyle\overset{def}{=}\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}\mathcal{A}(e,g_{1},\ldots,g_{k},h_{1},\ldots,h_{k}) $$

We can now note that if for a fixed value of $e$ , if in the asymptotic limit of $n,m\rightarrow\infty$ that $\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\bar{\mathcal{A}}$ converges to some fixed value, the CGMT guarantees that $\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\bar{\mathcal{A}}$ . This implies pointwise convergence on the set $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ , we can further establish uniform convergence by noting that $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ is compact, and that $\mathcal{P}$ is Lipschitz with respect to $e$ , implying equicontinuity. Classical results from analysis guarantee uniform convergence in these cases. As such we drop the outer parenthesis and consider the joint minimization over $e,Z$ in the analysis of $\mathcal{A}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\min_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z},e\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}\max_{\Lambda\in\mathcal{S}_{\Lambda}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}\left\|\lambda_{l}\right\|g_{l}^{T}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}e+\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}\left\|\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e\right\|h_{l}^{T}\lambda_{l} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}z_{l}-\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}\nu_{l}+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})+R(\mathbf{e}+\theta^{*}) $$

We now define $p_{l}=\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e$ , and reintroduce this constraint using the Lagrange multiplier $\mu_{l}$ . We can note for each each $p_{l}$ that $\left\|p_{l}\right\|\leq\sqrt{\sigma_{max}(\Sigma_{l})}\left\|e\right\|$ , by noting that $\Sigma_{l}$ has finite maximum singular value, and the bounds on $\left\|\mathbf{e}\right\|$ , we can conclude that there exists a compact set $\mathcal{S}_{P}=\set{P\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}{\ \left\|P\right\|_{2}\leq C_{P}\sqrt{d}}$ , where $P$ has columns $p_{l}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\min_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z},e\in\mathcal{S}_{e},P\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}\max_{\Lambda\in\mathcal{S}_{\Lambda},M}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}\left\|\lambda_{l}\right\|g_{l}^{T}p_{l}+\frac{1}{nk\sqrt{d}}\left\|p_{l}\right\|h_{l}^{T}\lambda_{l} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}z_{l}-\frac{1}{nk}\lambda_{l}^{T}\nu_{l}+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})+\frac{1}{dk}\mu_{l}^{T}(p_{l}-\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e)+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

where $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ has columns $\mu_{l}$ .

We now let $\beta_{l}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left\|\Lambda_{l}\right\|$ and solve over $\lambda_{l}$ , as shorthand we will define $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ , with elements $\beta_{l}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\min_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z},e\in\mathcal{S}_{e},P\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}\max_{\beta\succeq 0,M}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}}{k\sqrt{nd}}g_{l}^{T}p+\frac{\beta_{l}}{k\sqrt{n}}\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\left\|p_{l}\right\|_{2}h_{l}+z_{l}-\nu_{l}\right\|_{2} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})+\frac{1}{dk}\mu_{l}^{T}(p_{l}-\Sigma^{1/2}e)+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

We now interchange the order of min and max, let $\xi_{l}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\left\|p_{l}\right\|_{2}$ , and solve over $P$ . We obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\beta\succeq 0,M}\min_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z},e\in\mathcal{S}_{e},\xi\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}}{\sqrt{n}k}\left\|\xi_{l}h_{l}+z_{l}-\nu_{l}\right\|_{2}-\frac{\xi_{l}}{k\sqrt{d}}\left\|\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\beta_{l}\mathbf{g}_{l}+\mu_{l}\right\|_{2} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})-\frac{1}{dk}\mu_{l}^{T}\Sigma^{1/2}e+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

Recalling the square-root trick, where for any vector $a$ , we can note that $\left\|a\right\|_{2}=\min\limits_{q>0}\frac{q}{2}+\frac{\left\|a\right\|^{2}}{2q}$ . We apply the square root trick twice to the optimization above with parameters $q_{l}$ and $r_{l}$

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\beta,r\succeq 0,M}\min_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{Z},e\in\mathcal{S}_{e},\xi,q\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}+\frac{\beta_{l}}{2nkq_{l}}\left\|\xi_{l}h_{l}+z_{l}-\nu_{l}\right\|^{2}_{2}-\frac{\xi_{l}}{2kdr_{l}}\left\|\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\beta_{l}g_{l}+\mu_{l}\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{nk}\ell_{l}(z_{l})-\frac{1}{kd}\mu_{l}^{T}\Sigma^{1/2}e+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

We can now recognize the Moreau envelopes over $\ell_{l}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\beta,r\succeq 0,M}\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e},\xi,q\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}}{2kmr_{l}}\left\|\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\beta_{l}g_{l}+\mu_{l}\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{nk}\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \ell_{l}}\left(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}\right)-\frac{1}{kd}\mu_{l}^{T}\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

We once again interchange the order of min and max and now solve over $\mu_{l}$ . We can find that the optimal solution is given by:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{l}=-\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\beta_{l}g_{l}-\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma^{1/2}_{l}e $$

Substituting in this value we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\xi,q\succeq 0}\max_{\beta,r\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}+\frac{1}{nk}\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \ell_{l}}\left(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}\right) \displaystyle+\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}\frac{1}{2d}e^{T}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{k}}\Sigma_{l}\right)e+\frac{1}{d}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\beta_{l}\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}g_{l}\right)^{T}e_{l}+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

We can now complete the square over $e$ , from which we find that

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\xi,q\succeq 0}\max_{\bm{\beta},\mathbf{r}\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}+\frac{1}{nk}\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \ell_{l}}\left(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}\right)-\frac{1}{2kd}b^{T}A^{-1}b \displaystyle+\min_{e\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}\frac{1}{2d}\left(e+A^{-1}b\right)^{T}A\left(e+A^{-1}b\right)+R(e+\theta^{*}) $$

Where we have defined $A=\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{k}}\Sigma_{l}\right)$ and $b=\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\beta_{l}\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}\Sigma_{l}^{1/2}g_{l}\right)$ . We can note that $b^{T}A^{-1}b$ will concentrate to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{k^{2}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}d}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1} $$

We can now return $\theta=e+\theta^{*}$ as the optimization variable, and then recognize the Moreau envelope over $R$ , we obtain the optimization:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\bm{\xi},\mathbf{q}\succeq\mathbf{0}}\max_{\bm{\beta},\mathbf{r}\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}+\frac{1}{nk}\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \ell_{l}}\left(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}\right) \displaystyle-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{d}\mathcal{M}_{A^{-1}\ R}\left(\theta^{*}-A^{-1}b\right) $$

#### XI-A2 $\ell_{2}^{2}$ loss, and $\ell_{2}^{2}$ regularization

We consider the loss functions $\frac{1}{2}\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}^{2}$ . For the regularization we will consider the following function

$$ \displaystyle R(\theta)=\frac{\lambda}{2d}\left\|\theta\right\|_{2}^{2} $$

where $\lambda$ is a regularization parameter. We will assume that the noise $\nu_{l}$ will be distributed normally, by $\nu_{l}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\nu,l}^{2}I)$ . We can find the following results:

#### $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}$ loss

In this case we have:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}^{2}}(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l})=\min_{z_{l}}\frac{1}{2}\left\|z_{l}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\beta_{l}}{2q_{l}}\left\|\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}-z_{l}\right\|_{2}^{2} $$

We can find the optimal solution to be given by:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{z_{l}}=\frac{\beta_{l}}{\beta_{l}+q_{l}}(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l}) $$

Similarly we can find the optimal value to be:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}^{2}}(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l})=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\frac{\beta_{l}}{\beta_{l}+q_{l}}(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l})\right\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\beta_{l}}{2q_{l}}\left\|\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}+q_{l}}\nu_{l}-\frac{q_{l}\xi_{l}}{\beta_{l}+q_{l}}h_{l}\right\|_{2}^{2} $$

This concentrates on its expected value, given by:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{M}_{\frac{q_{l}}{\beta_{l}}\ \left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}^{2}}(\nu_{l}-\xi_{l}h_{l})=\frac{n}{2}\frac{\beta_{l}}{\beta_{l}+q_{l}}(\sigma_{\nu,l}^{2}+\xi_{l}^{2}) $$

#### Regularization Function

We can find that the regularization function in this case take the form

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{A^{-1}\ R}\left(\theta^{*}-A^{-1}b\right)=\min_{\theta}\frac{\lambda}{2d}\left\|\theta\right\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2d}\left(\theta-\theta^{*}+A^{-1}b\right)A(\theta-\theta^{*}+A^{-1}b) $$

From this we can find that the optimal value for $\theta$ is given by:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}=\mathrm{prox}_{A^{-1}\ R}\left(\theta^{*}-A^{-1}b\right)=(\lambda I+A)^{-1}\left(A\theta^{*}-b\right) $$

We also find that the optimal value in this case is given by:

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2d}\left(A\theta^{*}-b\right)\left(\lambda I+A\right)^{-1}\left(A\theta^{*}-b\right)+\frac{1}{2d}\theta^{*}A\theta^{*}+\frac{1}{d}\theta^{*T}b+\frac{1}{2d}b^{T}A^{-1}b $$

We can note that this concentrates to:

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2d}\theta^{*T}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)\theta^{*} \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2dk^{2}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}d}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{2dk}\theta^{*}\left(\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)\theta^{*} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{k^{2}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1} $$

As such we have as our total optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\xi,q\succeq 0}\max_{\beta,r\succeq 0}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}q_{l}}{2k}-\frac{\xi_{l}r_{l}}{2k}+\frac{n}{2}\frac{\beta_{l}}{\beta_{l}+q_{l}}(\sigma_{\nu,l}^{2}+\xi_{l}^{2}) \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2dk^{2}}\theta^{*T}\left(\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)\theta^{*} \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2dk^{2}}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}d}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{2dk}\theta^{*T}\left(\sum_{l=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l}}{\xi_{l}}\Sigma_{l}\right)\theta^{*} $$

#### Generalization Error

We note that the generalization error is given by:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{l=1}^{k}\left\|y_{k,new}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}g_{k,new}^{T}\Sigma^{1/2}_{k}\hat{\theta}\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{k}\sigma_{\nu,k}^{2}-\frac{2}{d}\theta^{*T}\left(\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1}\Sigma_{l}\theta^{*}+\frac{1}{d}\theta^{*T}\Sigma_{l}\theta^{*} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{d}\theta^{*T}\left(\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1}\Sigma_{l}\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)\theta^{*} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2k^{2}}\frac{\beta_{l}^{2}}{n}\text{Tr}\Sigma_{l}\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1}\Sigma_{l}\left(\lambda I+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{r_{l^{\prime}}}{\xi_{l^{\prime}}}\Sigma_{l^{\prime}}\right)^{-1} $$

Where we have made use of the optimal value of $\hat{\theta}$ given in equation (21).

### XI-B Binary Classification for GMMs with arbitrary covariance matrices

The following trick will be of use for the purposes of the present section:

The square root trick. If $x>0$ , then its square root can be "linearized" as follows:

$$ \sqrt{x}=\min_{\beta>0}\frac{1}{2\beta}+\frac{\beta x}{2} $$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}rI+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\Sigma_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}I) $$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\sim(\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}rI+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\Sigma_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}I)^{\frac{1}{2}}G\text{ where }G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) $$

$$ \displaystyle\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\right]^{T}(\lambda I+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\Sigma_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\Sigma_{2})^{-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\right]= \displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\right]^{T}(\lambda I+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\Sigma_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\Sigma_{2})^{-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\right]\right)= \displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\right]\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}\Sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}_{i}g_{i}+\frac{n\beta_{i}\gamma_{i}}{4\tau_{i}}\mu_{i}\right]^{T}(\lambda I+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\Sigma_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\Sigma_{2})^{-1}\right)= \displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left((\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}rI+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\Sigma_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}I)(\lambda I+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\Sigma_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\Sigma_{2})^{-1}\right)= \displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left((\lambda I+\frac{n\beta_{1}}{4\tau_{1}}\Sigma_{1}+\frac{n\beta_{2}}{4\tau_{2}}\Sigma_{2})^{-1}(\frac{n^{2}\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{8\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}rI+\sum_{i=1}^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\Sigma_{i}+\frac{n^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}\gamma_{i}^{2}}{16\tau_{i}^{2}}I)\right) $$

#### XI-B3 Classification Error

An attentive reader might have noticed that we held up the classification error derivations to this point. Recall that the classification error for a weight $\hat{w}$ and a general GMM is given by:

$$ E(\hat{w})=\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{\mu_{1}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{1}\hat{w}}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}Q\left(-\frac{\mu_{2}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{2}\hat{w}}}\right) $$

The proof is a straightforward calculation but we provide it here for completeness:

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ E(\hat{w})=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{1},\Sigma_{1})}(\hat{w}^{T}x<0)+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{2},\Sigma_{2})}(\hat{w}^{T}x>0) $$

Subtracting the means from the sample point we have: $x=\mu_{1}+\eta_{1}$ for $x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{1},\Sigma_{1})$ and $x=\mu_{2}+\eta_{2}$ for $x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{2},\Sigma_{2})$ we obtain:

$$ E(\hat{w})=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\eta_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{1})}(\hat{w}^{T}y_{1}<-\mu_{1}^{T}\hat{w})+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\eta_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{2})}(\hat{w}^{T}\eta_{2}>-\mu_{2}^{T}\hat{w}) $$

Noticing that $\hat{w}^{T}\eta_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,w^{T}\Sigma_{1}w)$ and $\hat{w}^{T}\eta_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,w^{T}\Sigma_{2}w)$ we derive:

$$ \displaystyle E(\hat{w})=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\zeta_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{1}\hat{w})}(\zeta_{1}<-\mu_{1}^{T}\hat{w})+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\zeta_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{2}\hat{w})}(\zeta_{2}>-\mu_{2}^{T}\hat{w})= \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\xi_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}(\xi_{1}<-\frac{\mu_{1}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{1}\hat{w}}})+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\xi_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}(\xi_{2}>-\frac{\mu_{2}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{2}\hat{w}}})= \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}Q\left(\frac{\mu_{1}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{1}\hat{w}}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}Q\left(-\frac{\mu_{2}^{T}\hat{w}}{\sqrt{\hat{w}^{T}\Sigma_{2}\hat{w}}}\right) $$

∎

The classification error part for Theorem 6 follows immediately then by the definitions of $\gamma_{i}$ and $\Theta_{i}$ for that case. We now proceed to derive the expressions for the classification error for Theorem 7 and Corollary 2. Note that by definition

# One-Bit Quantization and Sparsification for Multiclass Linear Classification via Regularized Regression

**Authors:** Reza Ghane* Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Affiliation: Pasadena, CA 91125 Email: rghanekh@caltech.edu Danil Akhtiamov* Affiliation: Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Affiliation: Pasadena, CA 91125 Email: dakhtiam@caltech.edu Babak Hassibi Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Affiliation: Pasadena, CA 91125 Email: hassibi@caltech.edu

## Abstract

We study the use of linear regression for multiclass classification in the over-parametrized regime where some of the training data is mislabeled. In such scenarios it is necessary to add an explicit regularization term, $\lambda f(w)$ , for some convex function $f(\cdot)$ , to avoid overfitting the mislabeled data. In our analysis, we assume that the data is sampled from a Gaussian Mixture Model with equal class sizes, and that a proportion $c$ of the training labels is corrupted for each class. Under these assumptions, we prove that the best classification performance is achieved when $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|^{2}_{2}$ and $\lambda\to\infty$ . We then proceed to analyze the classification errors for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ and $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ in the large $\lambda$ regime and notice that it is often possible to find sparse and one-bit solutions, respectively, that perform almost as well as the one corresponding to $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ .

A Preprint

## 1 Introduction

While large neural networks, such as Large Language Models (LLMs), have increasingly become an indispensable part of almost every inference task, their impressive performance comes at the price of enormous scale. To name a few, Llama 2 and GPT-4 are each comprised of 65 billion and 1.76 trillion parameters, respectively. Such models suffer from the common issues pertaining to their size: they require very large memory for storage, can consume inordinate amounts of power, and it can be very inefficient to communicate them over communication networks. This calls for the development of efficient methods for model quantization and pruning, where quantization refers to the us of a small number of bits to store each model parameter, and where pruning refers to setting some of the parameter values to zero. While multiple papers suggesting such methods have appeared recently (see, e.g.. Frantar and Alistarh, 2023a (); Frantar and Alistarh, 2023b (); Wang et al., (2023); Shang et al., (2023) and the references therein), we have very little understanding of the theoretical limitations of such methods. In other words, one would like to have an answer to the following question: for a given model and data set, how much does one have to sacrifice in performance if instead of looking at all potential solutions one looks only at, say, solutions of a given sparsity, or solutions where the weights are quantized to a certain level, such as one-bit? Of course, this question remains wide open for general supervised machine learning problems. As a first step in this direction, we will investigate it in the context of multiclass linear classification using regularized linear regression.

Multiclass classifiers play a crucial role in numerous machine learning applications. In fact, it can be argued that the power of deep learning manifests itself most prominently in the multiclass setting. Many image databases, for example Deng et al., (2009), contain tens of classes which any classifier will need to contend with. Multiclass classification further arises in problems with categorical outputs, such as natural language processing Sutskever et al., (2014), in reinforcement learning Jang et al., (2016), where the agent has to choose the correct action among a large set of possible ones, in recommendation systems Covington et al., (2016), and in many others.

Despite the widespread use and success of multiclass classification, we still have a rather poor understanding of the theory behind their performance. There are many pertinent questions for which we do not have answers. For example, what is the classification error? How does it depend on the number of classes? How does it depend on the loss function and the regularizer being used in the training? What are the best algorithms for finding good sparse or good compressed classifiers? Can we determine the best possible generalization performance among all solutions of given sparsity, or among all solutions where each parameters is quantized to a single bit? Can we efficiently learn these from data? What is the best one can do on a dataset with label corruption? Currently, we are quite far from satisfactorily answering any of these questions.

A common feature of modern successful multiclass classifiers is that they are highly over-parametrized. In fact, the number of parameters that needs to be trained is often orders of magnitude larger than the number of training samples. In this setting, models can easily interpolate the training data and classical learning theory would raise the concern of “over-fitting" and loss of generalization performance. In practice, however, the opposite has been often observed—increasing the parameters in the model improves generalization performance, a phenomenon referred to as “double descent" Belkin et al., (2020). It is now largely agreed upon that, the reason why over-fitting does not arise is that the (stochastic) gradient-based methods that are used to train over-parametrized models possess “implicit bias" and ostensibly find “good" interpolating solutions Gunasekar et al., (2017); Azizan and Hassibi, (2019); Azizan et al., (2021); Gunasekar et al., 2018a (); Gunasekar et al., 2018b (). Nonetheless, the precise relationship between implicit bias and classification error is not well understood. For example, it has been observed that changing the training algorithm can change the implicit bias, and thereby the classification error Azizan et al., (2021). However, the relationship between implicit bias and generalization is not known and is not clear what type of implicit bias will lead to good generalization performance. Furthermore, the theoretical analysis of double descent (see, e.g., Belkin et al., (2020); Deng et al., (2022) becomes less responsive when it comes to having a training dataset that contains mislabeled data. Given the described challenges, in this paper we will focus our study on a special case that is much more amenable to analysis, namely multiclass linear classifiers, hoping that the insights obtained will be informative for more general multiclass classifications settings.

In particular, we assume that the data is sampled from a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with equal class sizes where a proportion $c$ of the training labels is corrupted for each class. Since we consider the over-parametrized regime, to avoid overfitting the mislabeled data we propose regularized linear regression with a regularizer $\lambda f(w)$ , for some convex function $f(\cdot)$ . Even this setting is rather challenging to analyze and so we focus our analysis on the regime of strong regularization, i.e., large $\lambda$ , where we can obtain precise expressions for the classification error of the solution corresponding to an arbitrary convex regularizer $f(\cdot)$ and an arbitrary number of classes. This is perhaps the most interesting case, because (as we show rigorously in the sequel) for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ it results in the best classification performance. Further, for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ we show that large $\lambda$ results in highly sparse sparse solutions with good performance, and that for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ large $\lambda$ results in solutions that can be compressed all the way to a single bit per parameter with little loss of performance. We also present numerical results validating the theory. Put together, our results suggest that in the over-parametrized regime, one can often find sparse or one-bit solutions without having to compromise much on performance even though the underlying data model has no inherent sparsity structure. We believe this observation might have significant theoretical implications for general over-parametrized models due to the common intuition that large neural networks tend to behave similarly to their first-order linear approximations.

## 2 Related works

In the case of binary classification, there has been a recent surge of results that provide a sharp analysis for a variety of methods tailored to different models (see, e.g., Thrampoulidis et al., 2018a (); Huang, (2017); Candès and Sur, (2018); Sur and Candès, (2019); Kammoun and Alouini, (2020); Salehi et al., (2019); Taheri et al., (2020); Deng et al., (2019); Montanari et al., (2019); Mignacco et al., (2020); Lolas, (2020); Akhtiamov et al., (2023) and the references therein). These works typically pose the over-parameterized binary classification problem as an optimization problem and employ the Convex Gaussian Min-Max Theorem (CGMT) Thrampoulidis et al., (2015); Thrampoulidis et al., 2018a (); Stojnic, (2013); Gordon, (1985) to obtain formulas for the classification error that involve solutions to a system of non-linear equations (in a small number of variables) that often do not admit closed-form expressions. These results follow a long line of work that deals with obtaining sharp high-dimensional asymptotics of convex optimization-based estimators.

While the above works have significantly advanced our understanding of binary classification in the over-parameterized regime, they do not shed much light on the multiclass setting. Four interesting recent papers that study the multiclass setting include Wang et al., (2021); Subramanian et al., (2022); Loureiro et al., (2021); Thrampoulidis et al., (2020).

Wang et al., (2021) establishes that in certain over-parameterized regimes the solution to a multiclass supprt vector machine (SVM) problem is identical to the one obtained by minimum-norm interpolation of one-hot encoded labels (equivalently, that gradient descent on squared loss leads to the same solution as gradient descent on cross-entropy loss, since the solution is determined by the implicit bias of these algorithms, not of the loss). In addition, Wang et al., (2021) shows that the multiclass problem with finitely many classes reduces to a finite set of pairwise competitions, all of which must be won for multiclass classification to succeed. Subramanian et al., (2022) establishes that multiclass classification qualitatively behaves like binary classification, as long as there are not too many classes. It further makes note that the key difference from the binary classification setting is that, as the number of classes increases, there are relatively fewer positive training examples of each class, making the multiclass problem “harder" than the binary one. We remark that the settings of Wang et al., (2021) and Subramanian et al., (2022) differ from ours: they consider a 1-sparse noiseless model of the labels, and a bi-level ensemble model for the different classes. We instead consider a Gaussian mixture model for the different classes.

Thrampoulidis et al., (2020) provided the first precise analysis of linear multi-class classification in the high-dimensional regime. Their work revealed that the classification accuracy depends on certain quantities, such as the correlation between the trained weights for each class, as well as the correlation between the trained weights and the means of the underlying distributions for each class. Computing these quantities is quite challenging and Thrampoulidis et al., (2020) is only able to do so for pure least-squares classifiers and for least-squares classifiers with $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ regularization.** * Thrampoulidis et al., (2020) uses CGMT and a full analysis of the multiclass classification problem requires a matrix generalization of the CGMT which currently does not exist. Also, they did not consider any label corruption, which would further impede the analysis.

Loureiro et al., (2021) use the celebrated replica method as intuition in order to derive an AMP (approximate message passing) sequence capturing the performance of the multiclass classification problem for an arbitrary convex loss function and an arbitrary convex regularizer. This way, Loureiro et al., (2021) expresses the classification error in terms of a few scalar quantities that can be determined from a low-dimensional system of saddle-point equations. Their analysis shows that, if the means of the GMM are sparse, then strong $\ell_{1}$ regularization improves performance. However, we show that, even when the means of the underlying GMMS are not sparse, strong $\ell_{1}$ regularization can lead to sparse solutions without sacrificing too much on classification performance. Furthermore, Loureiro et al., (2021) does not study the use of regularization for model compression and also do not consider any corruption in the labels. Finally, the methods developed in our work use CGMT and are therefore entirely different, in addition to being quite explicit in the large $\lambda$ regime. From this vantage point, they could be of independent interest in their own right.

## 3 Setup and preliminaries

### 3.1 The Gaussian mixture model with corruption

We will assume that we have $k$ classes, $n$ training samples, and that the training data is given by $\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ , where each $x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is an input, and $y_{i}$ is the corresponding (potentially corrupted) class label. We will further assume that the $x_{i}$ are generated in an iid fashion from a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), the data points are drawn uniformly from each class and the labels are corrupted in a uniform manner at a fixed rate $c<\frac{1}{k-1}$ . In other words, denoting the true label designating the class to which $x_{i}$ belongs by $\tilde{y_{i}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{Prob}(\tilde{y}_{i}=\ell)=\frac{1}{k} \displaystyle\mbox{Prob}(y_{i}=\ell)=\begin{cases}1-c,&\ell=\tilde{y}_{i}\\
\frac{c}{k-1},&\ell\neq\tilde{y}_{i}\end{cases}~~~\mbox{and}~~~x_{i}\sim{\cal N}(\mu_{\tilde{y_{i}}},\sigma^{2}I), $$

i.e. the inputs for each class $\ell$ are drawn from an isotropic multi-variate Gaussian distribution with mean $\mu_{\ell}$ and variance $\sigma^{2}I$ . We will find it useful to aggregate the mean vectors into the $k\times d$ matrix

$$ M^{T}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}\mu_{1}&\mu_{2}&\ldots&\mu_{k}\end{array}\right] $$

If we further define the $n\times d$ and $n\times k$ matrices

$$ \displaystyle X^{T}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}x_{1}&x_{2}&\ldots&x_{n}\end{array}\right],\quad\tilde{Y}^{T}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}e_{\tilde{y}_{1}}&e_{\tilde{y}_{2}}&\ldots&e_{\tilde{y}_{n}}\end{array}\right] \displaystyle Y^{T}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}e_{y_{1}}&e_{y_{2}}&\ldots&e_{y_{n}}\end{array}\right] $$

where $e_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ is the $\ell$ -th standard basis vector in $k$ -dimensional space. We may write

$$ X=\tilde{Y}M+A, $$

where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ has iid ${\cal N}(0,\sigma^{2})$ entries.

As one may expect, the performance of multiclass classification for the GMM model highly depends on the relative positions of the means $\mu_{\ell}$ . While it is possible to analyze general $\mu_{\ell}$ , we will assume that the $\mu_{\ell}$ are generated acoording to Assumpion A2 in Section 4.1. This assumption implies that $\mu_{\ell}^{T}\mu_{\ell^{\prime}}\approx r\|\mu_{\ell}\|\cdot\|\mu_{\ell^{\prime}}\|$ , for every $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ , i.e., that the mean vectors are pairwise equiangular.

### 3.2 Why considering GMMs is not too limiting: Gaussian Universality

While it might seem at first that the GMM assumption is very restrictive, due to Gaussian universality, this is not really the case. Put in our context, intuitively this says that for a large class of mixtures of $k$ distributions modeling the classes, replacing those with the GMM having the same means and covariances for each class will lead to asymptotically equal classification error as $n$ grows large. An interested reader can find a rigorous exposition and detailed related discussions in Dandi et al., (2023). To further illustrate this point, we conducted experiments exploring the performance of regularized linear models trained on MNIST and observed the performance to be very similar qualitatively to our predictions for GMMs (see Section J in the Appendix).

### 3.3 CGMT

The CGMT framework starts with a so-called primary optimization (PO) problem

$$ \min_{u\in S_{u}}\max_{v\in S_{v}}u^{T}Gv+\psi(u,v), $$

where $u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , $S_{u}$ and $S_{v}$ are convex sets, $\psi(\cdot,\cdot)$ is convex in its first argument and concave in its second one, and $G\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ has iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ entries. To analyze the (PO), the CGMT framework introduces the so-called auxilliary optimization (AO) problem

$$ \min_{u\in S_{u}}\max_{v\in S_{v}}\|u\|_{2}g^{T}v+\|v\|_{2}h^{T}u+\psi(u,v), $$

where $g\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ have iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ entries. Roughly speaking, the CGMT frameowrk states that, if, as $n\rightarrow\infty$ while keeping $\frac{d}{n}$ fixed, the optimum of (4) concentrates to some value $c$ , say, then the optimum of (3) concentrates to the same value. More importantly, if any Lipschitz function of the solution ${\hat{u}}_{AO}$ of (4), say its $\ell_{2}$ -norm, concentrates to some value, then the same Lipschitz function of the corresponding solution ${\hat{u}}_{PO}$ of (3) will concentrate to the same value. In a nutshell properties of the solution to the (PO) can be inferred from properties of the solution to the (AO). The advantage of this approach is that analyzing the (AO) is usually much simpler than the (PO) since it contains two random vectors, rather than an entire random matrix. Details and much more rigorous statements, can be found in Thrampoulidis et al., (2015); Thrampoulidis et al., 2018a ().

### 3.4 Classification error for linear classifiers

We will be considering linear classifiers. Thus, let $W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ be the matrix of $k$ weight vectors $w_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , for $\ell=1,2,\ldots,k$ . Given a new input vector $x$ , the linear classifier will estimate its label according to:

$$ {\hat{y}}=\mbox{arg}\max_{\ell\in[k]}w_{\ell}^{T}x. $$

The per-class classification error is defined as

$$ P_{e|\ell}=\mbox{Prob}({\hat{y}}\neq y|y=\ell),~~~\ell=1,2,\ldots k $$

and the total classification error as

$$ P_{e}=\mbox{Prob}({\hat{y}}\neq y)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}P_{e|\ell}. $$

For $\ell=1,2,\ldots k$ , let $S_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}^{(k-1)\times(k-1)}}$ denote the symmetric positive semidefinite (psd) matrix whose $(i,j)$ -th entry, $i,j\neq\ell$ is given by $(S_{\ell})_{ij}=(w_{\ell}-w_{i})^{T}(w_{\ell}-w_{j})$ and let $S_{\ell}^{1/2}$ denote its psd square root. Further, let $t_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{k-1}$ denote a vector whose $i$ -th entry for $i\neq\ell$ is $(t_{\ell})_{i}=(w_{i}-w_{\ell})^{T}\mu_{\ell}$ . Then Thrampoulidis et al., (2020), shows that

$$ P_{e|\ell}=1-\mathbb{P}(S_{\ell}^{1/2}g\geq t_{\ell}), $$

where $g\in\mathbb{R}^{k-1}$ has iid $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$ entries.

We remark that probabilities of the form (7) and (8), can be straightforwardly computed via Monte Carlo simulation once $S_{\ell}^{1/2}$ and $t_{\ell}$ are known. However, due to the symmetry that arises from having pairwise equiangular means $\mu_{\ell}$ and isotropic variances $\sigma^{2}I$ , it turns out that

$$ P_{e}=P_{e|\ell}=Q_{k}\left(\frac{\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w_{\ell}-w_{\ell^{\prime}})}{\sigma\|w_{\ell}-w_{\ell^{\prime}}\|}\right), $$

for any $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ where

$$ \displaystyle Q_{k}(a)=\mathbb{P}((I+\frac{\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{T}}{1+\sqrt{k}})g\geq\mathds{1}\sqrt{2}a) $$

### 3.5 Overview of approach

The linear multi-class classifier just described needs a set of weight vectors for each class. These weights should be learned from the training data. In what follows, we will assume that the estimator of the weights is found from solving the following optimization problem

$$ \displaystyle\min_{W}\left[\|XW-Y\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}f(w_{\ell})\right]=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\min_{w_{\ell}}\left[\|Xw_{\ell}-Y_{\ell}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell})\right] $$

where $Y_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ denotes the $\ell$ -the column of $Y$ , i.e., the $i$ -th entry of $Y_{\ell}$ is one if the $i$ -th data point is labelled $\ell$ and zero otherwise, $f(\cdot)$ is a convex regularizer of the weights, and $\lambda>0$ is the regularization parameter. Note that, in principle, the statistics for each separate $w_{l}$ can be found by analyzing $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell}}\|Xw_{\ell}-Y_{\ell}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell})$ using CGMT. However, this approach cannot capture the cross-correlations between $w_{\ell}$ and $w_{\ell^{\prime}}$ for $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ . Thus, we adopt a different approach in the present paper: we still use CGMT, but only for the sake of simplifying (11) under assumption that $\lambda$ is large. After making the necessary simplifications, we proceed to analyze the simplified PO in the large $\lambda$ regime. We can capture the cross-correlations now because we can analyze the simplified PO directly. To proceed according to the described plan, we need to transform the objective first:

#### Lemma 3.1.

Let

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\Phi}_{\ell,s,t}(w)=\|\tilde{A}w\|^{2}+\frac{n}{k}\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+\frac{n}{k}\left[(w^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w^{T}a-s)^{2}\right]+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w^{T}b-t)^{2}+\lambda f(w) $$

Where $\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell}+\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\eta_{l}$ and $\tilde{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k-2)\times d},a,b,\eta_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are i.i.d. $\mathscr{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$ and $s,t$ are scalars defined in (17). Assume that $X$ is distributed according to (2). Then the distributions of the solutions for the following two optimization problems are identical:

$$ \min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\|Xw_{\ell}-Y_{\ell}\|_{2}^{2}+\|Xw_{\ell^{\prime}}-Y_{\ell^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell})+\lambda f(w_{\ell^{\prime}}) $$

$$ \min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\Phi_{\ell,s,t}(w_{\ell})+\Phi_{\ell^{\prime},t,s}(w_{\ell^{\prime}}) $$

The above lemma guarantees that, any scalar characteristics of the joint distribution of $w_{\ell}$ and $w_{\ell^{\prime}}$ in (11) can be found from the corresponding scalar characteristics in (14). Note that characterising only such pairwise joint distributions is enough according to subsection 3.4. Let us now introduce the following notation:

$$ \displaystyle F_{\ell}(w_{\ell})=\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell,\rho}(w_{\ell}):=\rho\|w_{\ell}\|_{2}^{2}+F_{\ell}(w_{\ell})+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) \displaystyle\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell}(w_{\ell}):=\sigma^{2}n\|w_{\ell}|^{2}+F_{\ell}(w_{\ell})+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

We first proceed to prove that (14) is sandwiched between $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell,\rho}(w_{\ell})+\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell^{\prime},\rho}(w_{\ell^{\prime}})$ and $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell}(w_{\ell})+\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell^{\prime}}(w_{\ell^{\prime}})$ for small enough $\rho>0$ and, moreover, $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell,\rho}(w_{\ell})+\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell^{\prime},\rho}(w_{\ell^{\prime}})$ and $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell}(w_{\ell})+\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell^{\prime}}(w_{\ell^{\prime}})$ take the same value as $\lambda\to\infty$ (cf. Appendix C). We use this to rigorously prove that solving either $\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\rho}$ , for small enough $\rho>0$ , or $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}$ yields the same classification error as the solution of (14) when $n\to\infty$ (cf. Theorem 4.2). After that, we solve $\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell,\rho}$ and $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell}$ to prove Theorems 4.3 , 4.4 and 4.6. Finally, we use the result of Theorem 4.3 to deduce Theorem 4.1.

## 4 Main Results

### 4.1 Assumptions and notation

We start with the assumptions. (A2) is not necessary but adding it makes the results much more explicit.

- (A1) The data is generated from a GMM with means $\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{k}$ and covariance matrix $\sigma^{2}I$ for each class.

- (A2) Each mean $\mu_{\ell}$ , $\ell=1,\dots,k$ is i.i.d. $\mathscr{N}(0,1)$ and matching coordinates of different means are correlated according to $\mathbb{E}(\mu_{\ell})_{i}(\mu_{\ell^{\prime}})_{i}=r$ for some $-1\leq r\leq 1$ and all $i=1,\dots,d$ whenever $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ .

- (A3) The ratio $\frac{d}{n}$ is fixed as $n\to\infty$ .

- (A4) The regularizer $f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ is convex and satisfies $f(w)\geq q(d)\|w\|_{2}$ for some $q:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ .

Finally, also denote

$$ \displaystyle s=\frac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{\frac{(k-2)(2c-\frac{kc^{2}}{k-1})}{k-1}}+\sqrt{\frac{k(2c-\frac{kc^{2}}{k-1})}{k-1}}\right] \displaystyle t=\frac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{\frac{(k-2)(2c-\frac{kc^{2}}{k-1})}{k-1}}-\sqrt{\frac{k(2c-\frac{kc^{2}}{k-1})}{k-1}}\right] $$

### 4.2 The optimal regularizer and $\lambda$

#### Theorem 4.1.

Assume that (A1)-(A3) hold and that either $\sigma^{2}=o(n)$ or $c=0$ . Then taking $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ and $\lambda\to\infty$ minimizes the classification error $P_{e}$ in (7) among regularizers satisfying (A4).

Informally, the theorem above says that if one wants to use regularized linear regression to solve a multiclass classification task in the presence of mislabeled data, the best one can do is to set $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ and take a very large $\lambda$ . This result is part of the reason for why we focus on strong regularization (large $\lambda$ ) in this paper.

### 4.3 The Sandwich Theorem for multiclass linear classification in the large $\lambda$ regime

To tackle the problem of analyzing (14) in the large $\lambda$ regime, we "sandwich" it between two optimization problems that are much easier to solve. After that, we prove that solutions of (14) and the problems that "sandwich" it match asymptotically. Recall the "sandwiching" optimization problems are $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell,\rho}(w_{\ell})+\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell^{\prime},\rho}(w_{\ell^{\prime}})$ for small enough $\rho>0$ and $\displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell}(w_{\ell})+\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\ell^{\prime}}(w_{\ell^{\prime}})$ . Denote the classification error obtained from (14) by $P_{e,\lambda}$ and that obtained by the upper bound sandwich problem by ${\bar{P}}_{e,\lambda}$ . Then the following instrumental theorem shows that finding the classification error for (14) reduces to finding the classification error for the upper bound problem.

#### Theorem 4.2.

Consider any $f$ satisfying (A4). For any $\epsilon>0,\delta>0$ , there exists a $N_{0},\lambda_{0}(N_{0})$ , such that for every $n>N_{0},\lambda>\lambda_{0}(N_{0})$

$$ \mathbb{P}(|P_{e,\lambda}-{\bar{P}}_{e,\lambda}|<\epsilon)>1-\delta $$

### 4.4 Main Theorems

We now present a rigorous characterization of the performance of multiclass classification based on regularized linear regression. We start with $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ :

#### Theorem 4.3.

(Ridge Regression) Assume that (A1)-(A3) hold. Then in the case of $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ we have that $\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}P_{e,\lambda}$ is equal to the following with probability approaching $1$ as $n\to\infty$ :

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}Q_{k}(\frac{d(\zeta-\gamma)(1-r)}{2d(\zeta-\gamma)^{2}(1+\frac{\sigma^{2}k}{n}-r)+2(\alpha-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}d}) $$

where $\zeta,\gamma,\alpha,\beta,\Delta$ are closed-form functions of $\lambda$ omitted here for brevity and written in full in the Appendix in Theorem E.1

As noted in Theorem 4.1, when $\lambda$ is large, the above classifier achieves optimal classification error among all regularized linear regression classifiers. However, it may not have other desirable properties, such as yielding sparse solutions. Thus, one might wonder about the classification error and the sparsity rate arising from the application of $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ . The following theorem addresses this question:

#### Theorem 4.4.

(LASSO Regression) Under the assumptions (A1)-(A3), for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $\lambda_{0}$ such that for all $\lambda\geq\lambda_{0}$ , the classification error corresponding to $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ can be described as follows as $n\to\infty$ :

$$ |P_{e,\lambda}-Q_{k}(\frac{n\sqrt{d}(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})R(\Xi)}{k|\Delta(\Xi)|})|<\epsilon $$

Where $\Xi,\Delta(\Xi)$ and $R(\Xi)$ are explicit functions of $\lambda$ and other parameters whose definitions are provided in the Appendix (cf. Theorem F.3) and $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}$ are the solutions to the following scalar optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}}-\frac{d(\Xi^{2}+\lambda^{2})R(\Xi)}{4n\sigma^{2}}+\frac{d\Xi\lambda}{2n\sigma^{2}\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}})+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}\left[-c\gamma_{1}-(k-1)\frac{\gamma_{1}^{2}}{4}-(1-c)\gamma_{2}-\frac{\gamma_{2}^{2}}{4}-s\gamma_{3}-\frac{\gamma_{3}^{2}}{4}-t\gamma_{4}-\frac{\gamma_{4}^{2}}{4}\right] $$

Moreover, the classifier is $\left\lceil dR(\Xi)\right\rceil=\left\lceil 2dQ(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})\right\rceil$ -sparse.

We also deduce the following corollary.

#### Corollary 4.5.

Assume (A1)-(A3) hold. Then the fraction of nonzero entries of the optimal $w$ for the case $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ goes to zero as $\lambda\to\infty$ .

This means that as $\lambda\to\infty$ , the classifier has a classification error of $Q_{k}(0)=\frac{k-1}{k}$ which is simply that of random guessing. Thus, the optimal classifier for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ occurs for some intermediate value of $\lambda$ . Another desirable property one might try to achieve is compressibility. It turns out that $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ pushes a big proportion of the weights to concentrate around $\pm\|w\|_{\infty}$ as $\lambda$ grows large. Formally, we have the following theorem and corollary:

#### Theorem 4.6.

( $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ - Regularization) Under the assumptions (A1)-(A3), the classification error $P_{e,\lambda}$ corresponding to $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ can be described as follows in the large $\lambda$ regime with probability approaching $1$ as $n\to\infty$ :

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}Q_{k}(\frac{\sqrt{d}(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})(1-R(\Xi))}{2k\sigma^{2}|\Delta|(\Xi)}) $$

Where $\Xi,\Delta(\Xi)$ and $R(\Xi)$ are explicit functions of $\lambda$ and other parameters whose definitions are provided in the Appendix (cf. Theorem H.1) and $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}$ are the solutions to the following scalar optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\delta\geq 0}\max_{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}}\delta+\frac{nd\delta^{2}\sigma^{2}R(\Xi)}{\lambda^{2}}-(1-R)\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4n\sigma^{2}}-\frac{d\delta\Xi}{\lambda\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{2n^{2}\sigma^{4}\delta^{2}}{\Xi^{2}\lambda^{2}})+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}\left[-c\gamma_{1}-(k-1)\frac{\gamma_{1}^{2}}{4}-(1-c)\gamma_{2}-\frac{\gamma_{2}^{2}}{4}-s\gamma_{3}-\frac{\gamma_{3}^{2}}{4}-t\gamma_{4}-\frac{\gamma_{4}^{2}}{4}\right] $$

Moreover, $\zeta$ of the coordinates of the weights are equal to $\frac{\delta}{\lambda}$ and $\zeta$ of the weights are equal to $-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}$ and the rest of them take values between $-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}$ and $\frac{\delta}{\lambda}$ with $\zeta=\left\lceil\frac{R(\Xi)}{2}\right\rceil=\left\lceil Q(\frac{2\delta\rho}{\lambda\Xi})\right\rceil$

The aforementioned theorem implies the following corollary, that says that in the limit $\lambda\to\infty$ exactly half of the weights concentrate at $-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}$ and the remaining half concentrate at $\frac{\delta}{\lambda}$ . Since the classification error $P_{e}$ does not change if one rescales all weights simultaneously, it means that one can replace the weights of the solutions for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ by their signs in the large $\lambda$ regime without affecting the performance.

#### Corollary 4.7.

Assume (A1)-(A3) hold and let $\zeta$ be defined as in the theorem above. Then $\zeta$ goes to $\frac{1}{2}$ as $\lambda$ goes to $\infty$ :

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\zeta=\frac{1}{2} $$

## 5 Numerical Simulations

To validate our theory numerically, we plot the classification error obtained by solving the regularized linear regression problem, as well as the predictions coming from the scalarizations of $\bar{\phi}$ for three different tuples of $(d,n,r,k,\sigma,c)$ and for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ , $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ and $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ against the corresponding value of $\lambda$ . As expected, the predictions deviate from the error quite drastically for the small values of $\lambda$ , start approaching it closer for intermediate values, and then match it almost perfectly as $\lambda$ grows large. To calculate the classification error (which we refer as "true error"), we solved (11) using CVXPY Diamond and Boyd, (2016); Agrawal et al., (2018) and evaluated the corresponding error via (7). We performed the latter procedure multiple times and then averaged the answer over the runs to mitigate the noise. For deriving the predictions, we used Theorems 4.3, 4.4 and 4.6. For plotting, we used the closed-form expressions provided in the theorem for the case of $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ , employed scipy.optimize.fmin initialized at $(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4})=(0.1,0.1,0.1,0.1)$ for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ and ran a grid search over $\delta$ using scipy.optimize.fmin initialized at $(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4})=(0.1,0.1,0.1,0.1)$ each time for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ (the value for the initializations was chosen arbitrarily and just turned out to always yield the correct parameters). We put and describe the plots for one tuple of $(d,n,k,c,r,\sigma)$ in the next subsections and the remaining plots can be found in Section J of the Appendix. We indicate the values for the corresponding tuples of $(d,n,r,k,\sigma,c)$ in the descriptions of the plots.

### 5.1 $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$

The numerical experiments we conducted for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ can be foind in Fig.1. As predicted, the true error decreases as $\lambda$ increases and starts matching the values predicted via $\bar{\phi}$ as $\lambda$ grows large. In addition, the plot suggests that solving $\bar{\phi}$ provides a lower bound for the true classification error over the entire $\lambda$ domain. We leave theoretical analysis of this phenomenon to future work.

*Figure 1: We took $d=750$ , $n=500$ , $k=5$ , $r=0.8$ , $c=0.3$ and $\sigma=1$ . The prediction underestimates the true error for smaller values of $\lambda$ but, as expected, matches it for larger ones.*

### 5.2 $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$

The results of our experiments for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ can be found in Fig.2. The plot on the top depicts three lines: the true classification error, the classification error of the sparsified solution, and the classification error prediction from Theorem 4.3. To obtain the sparsified solution, we predicted sparsity rate $R$ from our analysis of ${\bar{\phi}}$ , and then took the true solution of (11) and set the smallest $d(1-R)$ values of each $w_{\ell}$ to zero. The classification error predicted by analysis of ${\bar{\phi}}$ underestimates the true error for smaller values of $\lambda$ but matches it for larger ones. The sparsified solution performs worse than the true solution at first but they become closer and closer as $\lambda$ grows. As can be seen, the classification error becomes almost zero when $\lambda\approx 50$ , but then it starts going up until it reaches the moment when $W=0$ and therefore the error is equal to $\frac{k-1}{k}=0.8$ . The second plot depicts the predicted sparsity rate. As can be seen, we achieve $\approx 15X$ sparsification at $\lambda\approx 50$ , where the error is optimal and, in fact, very close to that obtained from ridge regression. Thus, we obtain 15X compression with minimal loss of performance. Finally, note that this $\lambda$ turns out to be large enough for the true error, the error of the sparsified solution, and the predicted error to match very closely.

*Figure 2: We took $d=750$ , $n=500$ , $k=5$ , $r=0.8$ , $c=0.3$ and $\sigma=1$ for these plots. They illustrate that for these parameters it is possible to sparsify the weights by 15X while keeping the classification error very low.*

### 5.3 $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$

We showcase the results of our experiments for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ in Fig.3. The plot on the top contains three lines: the true classification error of the solution $W$ we obtained by solving (11) directly, the classification error for the compressed version of $W$ , which we simply took to be $sign(W)$ due to the scaling invariance of the error function and permutation symmetry of the model, and the classification error prediction from Theorem 4.6. As expected, they differ at first, but start matching very closely for large values of $\lambda$ . The plot on the bottom shows the percentage of weights on the boundary for each $\lambda$ . As can be seen, it is almost $1$ at the end. Finally, unlike the $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ case, we do not observe a drop of performance after a certain $\lambda$ , so the classification error for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ behaves much more similarly to ridge regression. It should be noted, however, that this is only an empirical observation at this point. Analytically proving whether this is generally true or not is left for future work.

*Figure 3: We took $d=750$ , $n=500$ , $k=5$ , $r=0.8$ , $c=0.3$ and $\sigma=1$ for these plots. They illustrate that for these parameters it is possible to compress each weight to one bit while keeping the classification error very low.*

## 6 Conclusion

We have rigorously analyzed the performance of regularized linear regression for multi-class classification in the presence of labeling errors in the strong regularization regime. Theory and simulations suggest that the optimal classification error is found by ridge regression with large regularization parameter as well as that using $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ and $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{1}$ and regularization one can obtain one-bit and sparse solutions, respectively, with negligible loss of performance. Studying the implications of these results, and whether they generalize, to nonlinear regression models, such as deep neural networks, is an interesting topic for future study.
