## Appendix C Sandwiching Lemmas

To provide insights on why we consider the lower and upper bound optimization, we utilize CGMT. To do so, we analyze the terms containing $w_{\ell}$ and $w_{\ell^{\prime}}$ separately first. Without loss of generality we will consider only the one with $w_{\ell}$ . Starting from (12) for $\Phi_{\ell,s,t}(w_{\ell})$ , applying Fenchel dual to $\|\tilde{A}w_{\ell}\|^{2}$ , we obtain:

$$ \min_{w_{\ell}}\max_{u_{\ell}}u^{T}_{\ell}\tilde{A}w_{\ell}-\frac{\|u_{\ell}\|^{2}}{4}+\frac{n}{k}\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

Using CGMT for the objective above:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell}}\max_{u_{\ell}}w_{\ell}^{T}g^{(\ell)}\|u_{\ell}\|+u_{\ell}^{T}h^{(\ell)}\|w_{\ell}\|-\frac{\|u_{\ell}\|^{2}}{4}+\frac{n}{k}\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell})\text{, where }g^{(\ell)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d})\text{ and }h^{(\ell)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{n}) $$

It is straightforward to see that for the optimal $u_{\ell}$ one has $u_{\ell}=\frac{\eta_{\ell}}{\|h^{(\ell)}\|}h^{(\ell)}$ , where $\eta_{\ell}=\|u_{\ell}\|$ and the expression above turns into:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell}}\max_{\eta_{\ell}\geq 0}w_{\ell}^{T}g^{(\ell)}\eta_{\ell}+\eta_{\ell}\sigma\sqrt{n}\|w_{\ell}\|-\frac{\eta_{\ell}^{2}}{4}+\frac{n}{k}\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+\frac{n}{k}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

Optimizing over $\eta_{\ell}$ we get:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell}}(w_{\ell}^{T}g^{(\ell)}+\sigma\sqrt{n}\|w_{\ell}\|)_{\geq 0}^{2}+\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}\right]+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

In the above optimization, one can decompose the optimal solution into $w^{*}_{\ell}=\alpha g_{\ell}+w_{\ell}^{\perp}$ with $g^{T}_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{\perp}=0$ for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ . now, $w^{T*}_{\ell}g=\alpha\|g\|^{2}$ , and in the objective, $(w_{\ell}^{T}g^{(\ell)}+\sigma\sqrt{n}\|w_{\ell}\|)_{\geq 0}^{2}=(\alpha\|g\|^{2}+\sigma\sqrt{n}\|w_{\ell}\|)_{\geq 0}^{2}$ . Note that the optimal $w^{*}_{\ell}$ , to minimize the cost would always have $\alpha\leq 0$ , which shows $(w_{\ell}^{T}g^{(\ell)}+\sigma\sqrt{n}\|w_{\ell}\|)_{\geq 0}^{2}\leq n\sigma^{2}\|w_{\ell}^{*}\|^{2}$ . To formalize this idea, we introduce the following notations for the subsequent lemmas:

$$ F(w_{\ell})=\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}\right] $$

$$ \underline{\phi}_{\lambda}(w_{\ell}):=F(w_{\ell})+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

$$ \phi_{\lambda}(w_{\ell}):=(w_{\ell}^{T}g^{(\ell)}+\sigma\sqrt{n}\|w_{\ell}\|)_{\geq 0}^{2}+F(w_{\ell})+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

$$ \bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w_{\ell}):=\sigma^{2}n\|w\|^{2}+F(w_{\ell})+\lambda f(w_{\ell}) $$

Lemma C.1 shows the inequality relation among the $\phi_{\lambda},\underline{\phi}_{\lambda},\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}$ on which the proof of Theorem 4.2 relies heavily. Lemmas C.3 and C.2 complete the sandwiching argument by showing that the limit of the lower bound and the upper bound match.

#### Lemma C.1.

The following inequalities hold for any $\lambda$

$$ \min_{w}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)\leq\min_{w}\phi(w)\leq\min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w) $$

#### Proof.

The inequality on the left-hand side holds because $\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)\leq\phi(w)$ is satisfied for every $w$ . To justify the right hand side one, take $w_{*}=\arg min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)$ . Since $g$ is random Gaussian and $w_{*}$ is independent from it, $w_{*}^{T}g=0$ and $\min_{w}\phi(w)\leq\phi(w_{*})=\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w_{*})$ ∎

#### Lemma C.2.

The following limit $\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)$ exists, is finite and non-zero

#### Proof.

It suffices to show that $\Theta(\lambda):=\min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)$ is bounded from above and increases in $\lambda$ . To show the former, note that $\Theta(\lambda)\leq\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(0)=\frac{c^{2}}{k-1}+(1-c)^{2}+s^{2}+t^{2}$ . To show the latter, note that $\phi_{\lambda}$ is linear so by appealing to Danskin’s theorem, we take the derivative at the optimal point and observe that it is non-negative: $\Theta^{\prime}(\lambda)=f(w_{*})\geq 0$ ∎

#### Lemma C.3.

Assume that the regularizer $f(w)$ satisfies $\|w\|_{2}\leq q(d)f(w)$ for some $q:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ . Then the following equality holds:

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w) $$

#### Proof.

Note that $\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)\leq\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)$ is implied by the previous lemma. To prove the converse inequality, note that for the purposes of minimization we can restrict both $\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}$ and $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}$ to the unit ball for large enough $\lambda$ . Indeed, suppose the contrary and assume $\|w_{*}\|\geq 1$ can happen for arbitrary large $\lambda$ , we then have $\lambda f(w)\geq\lambda q(d)\|w\|\geq\lambda q(d)$ , which is not bounded as a function of $\lambda$ , giving us a contradiction. Also taking $\lambda\geq\sigma^{2}nq(d)$ , we write

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}(w)=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}F(w)+\lambda(\frac{\sigma^{2}n\|w\|^{2}}{\lambda}+f(w))\leq\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}F(w)+\lambda(\frac{\sigma^{2}n\|w\|}{\lambda}+f(w))\leq $$

$$ \leq\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}F(w)+\lambda(\frac{\sigma^{2}nq(d)}{\lambda}+1)f(w)\leq\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}F(w)+2\lambda f(w)=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}(w) $$

∎

## Appendix D Proof of Theorem 4.2

We first state the following key lemma which will be referred to multiple times in this section. We also suppress notation by setting $\Phi_{\ell}:=\Phi_{\ell,s,t}$

#### Lemma D.1.

Let $f(x,y):\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a convex function on a compact set $U$ . Take a $L$ -Lipschitz function $\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ . For $\epsilon>0$ , consider $f^{\epsilon}(x,y):=\epsilon\|x\|^{2}+\epsilon\|y\|^{2}+f(x,y)$ . Let $(x^{*},y^{*})$ be a minimum point of $f^{\epsilon}$ . Then the following inequality holds:

$$ \displaystyle f^{\epsilon}(x,y)\geq\min_{w,v}f^{\epsilon}(w,v)+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(x)-\psi(x^{*}))^{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(y)-\psi(y^{*}))^{2} $$

#### Proof.

We proceed by the same approach as Lemma 11 in Panahi and Hassibi, (2017). Since $(x^{*},y^{*})$ is a minimum point of $f^{\epsilon}$ , then $2\epsilon x^{*}\in-\partial_{x}f(x^{*},y^{*})$ and $2\epsilon y^{*}\in-\partial_{y}f(x^{*},y^{*})$ , then by convexity:

$$ \displaystyle f(x,y)-f(x^{*},y^{*})\geq-2\epsilon x^{T*}(x-x^{*})-2\epsilon y^{T*}(y-y^{*}) $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle f^{\epsilon}(x,y)-f^{\epsilon}(x^{*},y^{*})=\epsilon(\|x\|^{2}-\|x^{*}\|^{2})+\epsilon(\|y\|^{2}-\|y^{*}\|^{2})+f(x,y)-f(x^{*},y^{*})\geq \displaystyle\epsilon(\|x\|^{2}-\|x^{*}\|^{2})+\epsilon(\|y\|^{2}-\|y^{*}\|^{2})-2\epsilon x^{T*}(x-x^{*})-2\epsilon y^{T*}(y-y^{*})=\epsilon(\|x\|^{2}+\|x^{*}\|^{2}-2x^{T}x^{*})+\epsilon(\|y\|^{2}+\|y^{*}\|^{2}-2y^{T}y^{*}) $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle f^{\epsilon}(x,y)\geq f^{\epsilon}(x^{*},y^{*})+\epsilon\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}+\epsilon\|y-y^{*}\|^{2} $$

Now by Lipschitzness of $\psi$ , we have:

$$ \displaystyle f^{\epsilon}(x,y)\geq f^{\epsilon}(x^{*},y^{*})+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(x)-\psi(x^{*}))^{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(y)-\psi(y^{*}))^{2} $$

Which concludes the proof ∎

For ease of proof, we require the objectives in the lower bound optimization to be strongly convex. We achieve this by adding $\epsilon\|w\|^{2}$ to the objective $\min_{w_{\ell}}\Phi_{\ell}(w)$ for a small $\epsilon>0$ . It has been proved in Theorem 2 in Panahi and Hassibi, (2017) that for the LASSO regression, the solutions do not change much as $\epsilon$ is chosen to be small. Here we prove this statement for the large $\lambda$ regime for the regularizer satisfying Assumption (A4). Let us start by defining few notations. Let

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\ell}^{\epsilon}(w):=\Phi_{\ell}(w)+\epsilon\|w\|^{2} \displaystyle w_{\Phi_{\lambda}}:=argmin(\Phi_{\ell}(w)),\quad w_{\Phi^{\epsilon}_{\lambda}}:=argmin(\Phi^{\epsilon}_{\ell}(w)) $$

#### Lemma D.2.

Let $\eta>0$ be given then for a large enough $\lambda$ and any $L$ -Lipschitz function, If $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(w_{\Phi_{\lambda}}^{\epsilon})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$ , then $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(w_{\Phi_{\lambda}})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$

#### Proof.

Let $\lambda$ be large enough such that $\|w_{\Phi_{\lambda}}\|\leq 1$ which is proven in lemma C.3. Then by assumption (A4), there exists $\lambda^{\prime}$ such that $\epsilon\|w\|^{2}+\lambda f(w)\leq\lambda^{\prime}f(w)$ for all $w$ that $\|w\|\leq M<\infty$ . This follows as we only perform the optimization over the compact set $\mathcal{S}_{w}$ . Indeed, taking any $\lambda^{\prime}\geq\lambda+\frac{M\epsilon}{q(d)}$ , guarantees

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda)f(w)\geq\frac{M\epsilon}{q(d)}f(w)\geq M\epsilon\|w\|\geq\epsilon\|w\|^{2} $$

This implies for $w\in\mathcal{S}_{w}$

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\lambda^{\prime}}(w)\geq\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w) $$

Now, we adopt a similar approach to Thrampoulidis et al., (2015) and let

$$ \displaystyle J_{\eta}:=\{\alpha||\alpha-\alpha_{*}|>\eta\} $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w)\in J_{\eta}}\Phi_{\lambda^{\prime}}\geq\min_{\psi(w)\in J_{\eta}}\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon} $$

By lemma D.1,

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}\geq\min_{v}\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(v)+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(w)-\psi(w_{\Phi_{\lambda}}))^{2} $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w)\in J_{\eta}}\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}\geq\min_{v}\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(v)+\frac{\epsilon\eta^{2}}{L^{2}} $$

By applying the same reasoning as lemma C.3, we observe

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\Phi^{\epsilon}_{\lambda}(w)=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\min_{w}\phi_{\lambda}(w) $$

Now by taking $\lambda$ large enough we obtain $\min_{v}\Phi_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\epsilon}(v)\leq\min_{v}\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(v)+\epsilon^{\prime}$ with $\epsilon^{\prime}<\frac{\epsilon\eta^{2}}{L^{2}}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w)\in J_{\eta}}\Phi_{\lambda^{\prime}}>\min\Phi_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\epsilon}\geq\min\Phi_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}\geq\min\Phi_{\lambda^{\prime}} $$

As $\lambda^{\prime}\geq\lambda+\frac{M\epsilon}{q(d)}$ is arbitrary large, this shows that with high probability, $|\psi(w_{\Phi_{\lambda}})-\alpha_{*}|<\eta$ . ∎

Let us define $w_{-}:=w_{\ell}-w_{\ell^{\prime}}$ and $w_{+}:=w_{\ell}+w_{\ell^{\prime}}$ . Under this change of variable, note that the $F$ in the eq. (16) would become

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{F}(w_{+},w_{-}):=\frac{n}{2k}(\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell,\ell^{\prime}}[(w_{-}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}})^{2}+(w_{+}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{2c}{k-1})^{2}]+(w_{+}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c+\frac{c}{k-1}))^{2}+(w_{-}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c-\frac{c}{k-1}))^{2}+ \displaystyle(w_{+}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}-(1-c+\frac{c}{k-1}))^{2}+(w_{-}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(\frac{c}{k-1}-1+c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{+}^{T}a-s-t)^{2}+ \displaystyle(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{+}^{T}a-s+t)^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{+}^{T}b-s-t)^{2})+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{+}^{T}b-t+s)^{2}) $$

Define the following transformed optimizations:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-}):=\epsilon\|w_{+}\|^{2}+\epsilon\|w_{-}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{A}w_{+}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{A}w_{-}\|^{2}+\tilde{F}(w_{+},w_{-})+\lambda f(\frac{w_{+}+w_{-}}{2})+\lambda f(\frac{w_{+}-w_{-}}{2}) \displaystyle\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-}):=\epsilon\|w_{-}\|^{2}+\epsilon\|w_{+}\|^{2}+\tilde{F}(w_{+},w_{-})+\lambda f(\frac{w_{+}+w_{-}}{2})+\lambda f(\frac{w_{+}-w_{-}}{2}) \displaystyle\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-}):=(\epsilon+n\sigma^{2})\|w_{-}\|^{2}+(\epsilon+n\sigma^{2})\|w_{+}\|^{2}+\tilde{F}(w_{+},w_{-})+\lambda f(\frac{w_{+}+w_{-}}{2})+\lambda f(\frac{w_{+}-w_{-}}{2}) $$

Further we denote

$$ \displaystyle(\hat{w}_{-},\hat{w}_{+}):=argmin(\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon}) \displaystyle(\underline{w}_{-},\underline{w}_{+}):=argmin(\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}) \displaystyle(\bar{w}_{-},\bar{w}_{+}):=argmin(\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}) $$

The following Lemma is key in the proof of Theorem 4.2

#### Lemma D.3.

Let $\eta>0$ be given, then for a large enough $\lambda$ and any $L$ -Lipschitz function, If $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(\underline{w}_{-})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$ , then $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(\hat{w}_{-})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$ and $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(\bar{w})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow 0$ .

#### Proof.

As $\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon}$ is always greater than $\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}$ on every point in its domain the following inequality holds w.p.a 1:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon}\geq\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon} $$

By the previous lemma, the following inequality holds with probability 1.

$$ \displaystyle\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-})\geq\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(w_{-})-\psi(\underline{w}_{-}))^{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(w_{+})-\psi(\underline{w}_{+}))^{2})\geq\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}(\psi(w_{-})-\psi(\underline{w}_{-}))^{2} $$

Thus minimizing over the set $J_{\eta}$ results in

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-})\geq\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}+\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}\eta^{2} $$

By Lemma C.3 for large enough lambda, there exists $\tilde{\epsilon}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\min\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}\leq\min\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}+\tilde{\epsilon} $$

We can take $\tilde{\epsilon}<\frac{\epsilon}{L^{2}}\eta^{2}$ , wp 1. This implies

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-})\geq\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}+\frac{\tau}{2}\eta^{2}>\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon} $$

We also know that $\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}=\min_{w_{1},w_{2}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}$ , which implies the following bound

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}\geq\min\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon} $$

All in all, we have w.p.a 1

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon}>\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\tilde{\Phi}^{\epsilon} $$

This implies the solution $\psi(\hat{w}_{-})\notin J_{\eta}$ w.p.a 1 and thus $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(\hat{w}_{-})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$ . Now for the $\psi(\bar{w})$ , the following holds w.p.a 1:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}\geq\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon} $$

As $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}$ is always greater than $\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}$ on every point in its domain. Then one has from the inequality (21)

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}(w_{+},w_{-})\geq\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\underline{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}+\frac{\tau}{2}\eta^{2}>\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon} $$

To summarize,

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\psi(w_{-})\in J_{\eta}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon}>\min_{w_{-},w_{+}}\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}^{\epsilon} $$

Which implies $\psi(\bar{w})\notin J_{\eta}$ w.p.a 1 and $\mathbb{P}(|\psi(\bar{w})-\alpha_{*}|>\eta)\rightarrow 0$ . This concludes the proof ∎

Finally, using the previous results we can prove Theorem 4.2:

#### Proof.

(Proof of Theorem 4.2) By equation 9 we know that the classification error is characterized by $\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})$ and $\|w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})\|$ . Therefore, the proof of Theorem 4.2 follows by applying Lemma D.3 twice to the Lipschitz functions $\psi_{1}(x):=\|x\|$ and $\psi_{2}(x):=\mu_{1}^{T}x$ . ∎

#### Theorem E.2.

Assume that either $\sigma^{2}=o(n)$ or $c=0$ . Then taking $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ and $\lambda\to\infty$ yields performance that approaches the best possible among classification methods based on regularized regression with a convex regularizer $f(w)$ satisfying $f(w)\geq q(d)\|w\|_{2}$ for some $q:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ when $n\to\infty$ .

#### Proof.

Note that due to the symmetry w.r.t. to the permutation of $\tilde{\mu}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\mu}_{k}$ in the objective we can write

$$ \displaystyle w_{\ell}=\gamma\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}+\zeta\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}+w_{\ell}^{\perp} \displaystyle w_{\ell^{\prime}}=\gamma\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}+\zeta\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}+w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\perp} $$

Here $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ are some scalars depending on $\lambda$ and $w_{\ell}^{\perp},w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\perp}$ are the projections of $w_{\ell}$ and $w_{\ell^{\prime}}$ respectively onto the subspace orthogonal to the span of $\tilde{\mu}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\mu}_{k}$ . Denote $w_{-}^{\perp}=w_{\ell}^{\perp}-w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\perp}$ and $w_{-}=w_{\ell}-w_{\ell^{\prime}}=(\zeta-\gamma)(\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}})+w_{-}^{\perp}$ . If $c=0$ , then $w_{-}^{\perp}=0$ and we are done. Otherwise we have that $\sigma^{2}=o(n)$ . Then to evaluate the classification error we need to evaluate the following quantity and the bigger this quantity the lower the error is:

$$ \frac{\mu_{l}^{T}w_{-}}{\|w_{-}\|}=\frac{(\zeta-\gamma)\mu_{l}^{T}(\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}})}{\sqrt{(\zeta-\gamma)^{2}\|\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}+\|w_{-}^{\perp}\|^{2}}}=\frac{d(1-r)}{\sqrt{2d(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}-r)+\frac{\|w_{-}^{\perp}\|^{2}}{(\zeta-\gamma)^{2}}}}\leq\frac{d(1-r)}{\sqrt{2d(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}-r)}} $$

Let us evaluate the performance for the solution for $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ now. Using the notation and the expressions from the previous section and taking $\lambda$ to go to $\infty$ we deduce that

$$ \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\frac{\|w_{-}^{\perp}\|^{2}}{(\zeta-\gamma)^{2}}=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}2\frac{(\alpha-\beta)^{2}\sigma^{2}d}{(\zeta-\gamma)^{2}}=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}2k\frac{(s-t)^{2}\sigma^{2}d}{n\tilde{\lambda}(\zeta-\gamma)^{2}}=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}2k\frac{(s-t)^{2}\sigma^{2}d\tilde{\lambda}^{2}}{n\tilde{\lambda}^{2}(\frac{c}{k-1}-1)^{2}}=O(\frac{d}{n})=O(1) $$

Thus, since we are interested in studying the asymptotics of the error this term can be dropped from the denominator compared to $2d(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}-r)$ as $n\to\infty$ and we are done. ∎

$$ |P_{e,\lambda}-Q_{k}(\frac{n\sqrt{d}(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})R(\Xi)}{k|\Delta|(\Xi)})|<\epsilon $$

$$ \displaystyle\Xi^{2}:=\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}}(k-1)\gamma_{1}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+\gamma_{2}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}))+\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}}(2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(k-1)r+\frac{k}{n}\sigma^{2}(\gamma_{3}^{2}+\gamma_{4}^{2})) \displaystyle R(\Xi):=2Q(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}) \displaystyle\Delta^{2}(\Xi):=\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle+\frac{2\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle+\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime}-2\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle\Omega:=\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}^{2}(k-2)(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-1)r)+(\gamma_{1}^{2}+\gamma_{2}^{2})r+2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+2\frac{k}{n}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}\sigma^{2}\right] $$

Where $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}$ are the solutions to the following scalar optimization problem:

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}}-\frac{d(\Xi^{2}+\lambda^{2})R(\Xi)}{4\rho}+\frac{d\Xi\lambda}{2\rho\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}})+\frac{n}{k}\left[-c\gamma_{1}-(k-1)\frac{\gamma_{1}^{2}}{4}-(1-c)\gamma_{2}-\frac{\gamma_{2}^{2}}{4}-s\gamma_{3}-\frac{\gamma_{3}^{2}}{4}-t\gamma_{4}-\frac{\gamma_{4}^{2}}{4}\right] $$

#### Proof.

We break the proof into several steps, described in the following sections.

### F.1 Scalarization of $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}$

First, consider the following optimization for an arbitrary $\rho=n\sigma^{2}$ , to obtain the final result, we plug-in $\rho=n\sigma^{2}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)^{2}\right]+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell})+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell^{\prime}}(w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})^{2}+(w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}-(1-c))^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}a-t)^{2}+(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}b-s)^{2}\right]+\rho\|w_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell^{\prime}}) $$

Taking the Fenchel dual of each term and making use of the symmetry of the model, we arrive at the following:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell},w_{\ell^{\prime}}}\max_{\gamma}\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}[\gamma_{\ell,1}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,1}^{2}}{4}]+\gamma_{\ell,2}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,2}^{2}}{4}+\gamma_{\ell,3}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,3}^{2}}{4}\right]+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell,4}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,4}^{2}}{4}\right]+\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell^{\prime}}[\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},1}(w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})-\frac{\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},1}^{2}}{4}]+\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},2}(w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}-(1-c))-\frac{\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},2}^{2}}{4}\right]+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},3}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}a-t)-\frac{\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},3}^{2}}{4}+\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},4}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell^{\prime}}^{T}b-s)-\frac{\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},4}^{2}}{4}\right]+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell})+\rho\|w_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}+\lambda f(w_{\ell^{\prime}}) $$

Due to symmetry, we only consider the optimization over $w_{\ell}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell}}\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell,1}\sum_{r\neq\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\gamma_{\ell,2}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}+\gamma_{\ell,3}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}a+\gamma_{\ell,4}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}b\right]^{T}w_{\ell}+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}+\lambda\|w_{\ell}\|_{1} $$

We first tackle an equivalent scalar optimization:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{x}ax+\lambda|x|+\rho x^{2} $$

Taking derivative and solving for $x$ yields

$$ \displaystyle a+\lambda\partial|x|+2\rho x=0 $$

$$ \displaystyle x^{*}=\frac{1}{2\rho}ST(-a;\lambda):=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2\rho}(-a-\lambda)&-a-\lambda>0\\
\frac{1}{2\rho}(-a+\lambda)&-a+\lambda<0\\
0&o.w\end{cases} $$

Where $ST(x;c)$ is defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle ST(x;c):=\begin{cases}x-c&x>c\\
x+c&x<-c\\
0&o.w\end{cases} $$

The objective value would be

$$ \displaystyle\min_{x}ax+\lambda|x|+\rho x^{2}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2\rho}((-a^{2}-a\lambda)+(-\lambda a-\lambda^{2})+\frac{1}{2}(a+\lambda)^{2})&-a-\lambda>0\\
\frac{1}{2\rho}((-a^{2}+a\lambda)+(\lambda a-\lambda^{2})+\frac{1}{2}(a-\lambda)^{2})&-a+\lambda<0\\
0&o.w\end{cases} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}-\frac{1}{4\rho}(a+\lambda)^{2}&-a-\lambda>0\\
-\frac{1}{4\rho}(a-\lambda)^{2}&-a+\lambda<0\\
0&o.w\end{cases}=-\frac{1}{4\rho}ST^{2}(-a;\lambda) $$

Now we apply this result to our problem. First let us define the following vectors for both of the classes $\ell,\ell^{\prime}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\ell}:=\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell,1}\sum_{r\neq\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\gamma_{\ell,2}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}+\gamma_{\ell,3}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}a+\gamma_{\ell,4}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}b\right] \displaystyle\Psi_{\ell^{\prime}}:=\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},1}\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}+\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},2}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}+\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},3}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}a+\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},4}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}b\right] $$

Leveraging the assumptions on $\mu$ ’s, we observe that $Var(\tilde{\mu}_{i,r})=1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}$ and $\mathbb{E}\tilde{\mu}_{i,\mathscr{r}}\tilde{\mu}_{i,\mathscr{r}^{\prime}}=r$ . Therefore, taking $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\ell}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\frac{n}{k}\sqrt{(k-1)\gamma_{\ell,1}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+\gamma_{\ell,2}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n})+2\gamma_{\ell,1}\gamma_{\ell,2}(k-1)r+\frac{k}{n}\sigma^{2}(\gamma_{\ell,3}^{2}+\gamma_{\ell,4}^{2})}G:=\Xi G $$

Then plugging in

$$ \displaystyle w^{*}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2\rho}ST(-\frac{n}{k}(\gamma_{\ell,1}\sum_{r\neq\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\gamma_{\ell,2}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}+\gamma_{\ell,3}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}a+\gamma_{\ell,4}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}b);\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\rho}ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda) $$

Using this result, the optimization over w would achieve the following value:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{w_{\ell}}\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell,1}\sum_{r\neq\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\gamma_{\ell,2}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}+\gamma_{\ell,3}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}a+\gamma_{\ell,4}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}b\right]^{T}w_{\ell}+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}+\lambda\|w_{\ell}\|_{1}=\frac{-1}{4\rho}\|ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda)\|^{2} $$

Now using the concentration properties we calculate the expectation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda)\|^{2}=d\mathbb{E}ST^{2}(\Xi G;\lambda)=d\mathbb{E}(\Xi G-\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(\Xi G>\lambda)+d\mathbb{E}(\Xi G+\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(\Xi G<-\lambda)= \displaystyle 2\Xi^{2}d\mathbb{E}G^{2}\mathds{1}(\Xi G>\lambda)+2d\lambda^{2}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(\Xi G>\lambda)-2d\Xi\lambda\mathbb{E}G\mathds{1}(\Xi G>\lambda)+2d\Xi\lambda\mathbb{E}G\mathds{1}(\Xi G<-\lambda)= \displaystyle 2\Xi^{2}d\mathbb{E}G^{2}\mathds{1}(G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})+2d\lambda^{2}Q(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})-4d\Xi\lambda\mathbb{E}G\mathds{1}(G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})=2\Xi^{2}d\mathbb{E}G^{2}\mathds{1}(G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})+2d\lambda^{2}Q(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})-\frac{4d\Xi\lambda}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}})= \displaystyle 2d\lambda^{2}Q(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})-\frac{4d\Xi\lambda}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}})+2\Xi^{2}d(Q(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})+\frac{\lambda}{\Xi\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}}))= \displaystyle 2dQ(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})(\Xi^{2}+\lambda^{2})-\frac{2d\Xi\lambda}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}}) $$

Plugging back in, we get the following optimization

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\gamma_{\ell,1},\gamma_{\ell,2},\gamma_{\ell,3},\gamma_{\ell,4}}\frac{n}{k}\left[-c\gamma_{\ell,1}-(k-1)\frac{\gamma_{\ell,1}^{2}}{4}-(1-c)\gamma_{\ell,2}-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,2}^{2}}{4}-s\gamma_{\ell,3}-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,3}^{2}}{4}-t\gamma_{\ell,4}-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,4}^{2}}{4}\right]- \displaystyle-\frac{d(\Xi^{2}+\lambda^{2})R(\Xi)}{4\rho}+\frac{d\Xi\lambda}{2\rho\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\Xi^{2}}) $$

Where the quantity

$$ \displaystyle R(\Xi)=\mathbb{P}(|\Psi_{\ell}|=\Xi G\geq\lambda)=2Q(\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}) $$

is the the fraction of nonzero entries of the optimal $w$ .

### F.2 Derivation of the classification error

First note that by the derivation from previous section, $\|w_{\ell}-w_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}=\frac{1}{4\rho^{2}}\|ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda)-ST(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime}};\lambda)\|^{2}$ and $\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w_{\ell}-w_{\ell^{\prime}})=\frac{1}{2\rho}\mu_{\ell}^{T}(ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda)-ST(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime}};\lambda))$ . Furthermore, It can be seen that $\gamma_{\ell,1}=\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},1}=\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{\ell,2}=\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},2}=\gamma_{2}$ and $\gamma_{\ell,3}=\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},4}=\gamma_{3}$ and $\gamma_{\ell,4}=\gamma_{\ell^{\prime},3}=\gamma_{4}$ due to symmetry. In fact, one has

$$ \displaystyle(\Psi_{\ell,i},\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^{2}_{\ell}&r_{\ell}\\
r_{\ell}&\sigma^{2}_{\ell^{\prime}}\end{pmatrix}) $$

Where by symmetry, $\sigma^{2}_{\ell}=\sigma^{2}_{\ell^{\prime}}=\Xi^{2}$ , and for the correlation,

$$ \displaystyle\Omega:=\frac{1}{\Xi^{2}d}\mathbb{E}\Psi_{\ell}^{T}\Psi_{\ell^{\prime}}=\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}^{2}(\sum_{r\neq\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{r})^{2}+(\gamma_{1}^{2}+\gamma_{2}^{2})\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}\right]+\frac{n}{k\Xi^{2}}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}\left[a^{2}+b^{2}\right]+ \displaystyle+\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}^{2}+\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2})+\gamma_{1}^{2}(\sum_{r\neq\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\sum_{r\neq\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{r})+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(\sum_{r\neq\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\sum_{r\neq\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{r})\right]= \displaystyle=\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}^{2}(k-2)(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-3)r)+(\gamma_{1}^{2}+\gamma_{2}^{2})r+2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n})+2(k-2)r\gamma_{1}^{2}+2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(k-2)r+2\frac{k}{n}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}\sigma^{2}\right]= \displaystyle\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}^{2}(k-2)(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-3)r)+(\gamma_{1}^{2}+\gamma_{2}^{2})r+2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+2(k-2)r\gamma_{1}^{2}+2\frac{k}{n}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}\sigma^{2}\right]= \displaystyle\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}^{2}(k-2)(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-1)r)+(\gamma_{1}^{2}+\gamma_{2}^{2})r+2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+2\frac{k}{n}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}\sigma^{2}\right] $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle(\Psi_{\ell,i},\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\begin{pmatrix}\Xi^{2}&\Omega\Xi^{2}\\
\Omega\Xi^{2}&\Xi^{2}\end{pmatrix}) $$

And we can take $(\Psi_{\ell,i},\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(G,G^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\begin{pmatrix}1&\Omega\\ \Omega&1\end{pmatrix})$ . Now we focus on the calculation of the classification error which requires the characterization of $\frac{\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})}{\|w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell}\|}$ . Beginning with $\|w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell}\|$ , we have from concentration.

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\|ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda)-ST(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime}};\lambda)\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell,i}-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i})^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}>\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}>\lambda)\right]+ \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell,i}-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i})^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}<-\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}<-\lambda)\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell,i}+\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}>\lambda,|\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}|<\lambda)\right]+ \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}-\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(|\Psi_{\ell,i}|<\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}<-\lambda)\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}-\Psi_{\ell,i}-2\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}>\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}<-\lambda)\right]+ \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell,i}-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}+2\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}<-\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}>\lambda)\right]= \displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell,i}-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i})^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}>\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}>\lambda)\right]+4\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell,i}-\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}<-\lambda,|\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}|<\lambda)\right]+ \displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}\left[(\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}-\Psi_{\ell,i}-2\lambda)^{2}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}>\lambda,-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}<-\lambda)\right]=2\Xi^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\mathds{1}(G<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi},G^{\prime}<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})\right]+ $$

We calculate each term separately. Let $(G,G^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathcal{R})$ with $\mathcal{R}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\Omega\\ \Omega&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1-\Omega^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-\Omega\\ -\Omega&1\end{pmatrix}$ . Using this, one can write

$$ \displaystyle 2\Xi^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\mathds{1}(G<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi},G^{\prime}<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})\right]=\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})}) $$

$$ \displaystyle 4\Xi^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[(G-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\mathds{1}(G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi},|G^{\prime}|<\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})\right]=\frac{2\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})}) $$

$$ \displaystyle 2\Xi^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[(G-G^{\prime}+2\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\mathds{1}(G<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi},G^{\prime}>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})\right]=\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime}-2\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})}) $$

Combining results yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\|ST(-\Psi_{\ell};\lambda)-ST(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime}};\lambda)\|^{2}=\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle+\frac{2\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle+\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime}-2\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} $$

For the inner product, we utilize Lemma F.2 and calculate the each term in $\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})$ separately. First, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell}=\frac{d}{2\rho}\mathbb{E}\mu_{\ell,i}ST(-\Psi_{\ell,i};\lambda)=\frac{d}{2\rho}\sum_{\mathscr{r}=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\mu_{\ell,i}\mu_{\mathscr{r},i}\left[\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}>\lambda)\partial_{\mu_{\mathscr{r},i}}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}-\lambda)+\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}<-\lambda)\partial_{\mu_{\mathscr{r},i}}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}+\lambda)\right]= \displaystyle-\frac{dn}{2\rho k}(k-1)r\gamma_{1}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(|\Psi_{\ell,i}|>\lambda)-\frac{dn}{2\rho k}\gamma_{2}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(|\Psi_{\ell,i}|>\lambda)=-\frac{dn}{2\rho k}R((k-1)r\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}) $$

Also similarly,

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}=\frac{d}{2\rho}\mathbb{E}\mu_{\ell,i}ST(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i};\lambda)=\frac{d}{2\rho}\sum_{\mathscr{r}=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\mu_{\ell,i}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r},i}\left[\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}>\lambda)\partial_{\mu_{\mathscr{r},i}}(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}-\lambda)+\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(-\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}<-\lambda)\partial_{\mu_{\mathscr{r},i}}(-\Psi_{\ell,i}+\lambda)\right]= \displaystyle-r\frac{nd}{2\rho k}\gamma_{2}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(|\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}|>\lambda)-\frac{nd}{2\rho k}(k-2)r\gamma_{1}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(|\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}|>\lambda)-\frac{nd}{2\rho k}\gamma_{1}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(|\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}|>\lambda)=-\frac{nd}{2\rho k}R(\gamma_{1}(1+(k-2)r)+\gamma_{2}r) $$

Thus this yields the following

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})=-\frac{nd}{2\rho k}R(\gamma_{1}(1+(k-2)r)+\gamma_{2}r-(k-1)r\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})=-\frac{nd}{2\rho k}R(1-r)(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2}) $$

Therefore, summarizing,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})}{\|w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell}\|}=\frac{\frac{n\sqrt{d}}{k}R(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})}{|\Delta|(\Xi)} \displaystyle\Delta^{2}(\Xi):=\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle+\frac{2\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle+\frac{\Xi^{2}}{\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G>\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{\lambda}{\Xi}}(G-G^{\prime}-2\frac{\lambda}{\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} $$

Now we apply Theorem 4.2 and observe that with high probability, for a large enough $\lambda$ ,

$$ |P_{e,\lambda}-Q_{k}(\frac{n\sqrt{d}(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})R(\Xi)}{k|\Delta|(\Xi)})|<\epsilon $$

## Appendix G Proof of Corollary 4.5

By the result from Theorem D.4, we observe that the sparsity rate predicted for $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}$ and $\tilde{\Phi}$ can be made arbitrarily close as $\lambda\rightarrow\infty$ .

Now to prove the Corollary 4.5, observe that we have from the previous theorem:

$$ \displaystyle dR=\frac{2\rho k\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})}{n(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})} $$

First note that by the Fenchel dual argument,

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{1}=2(\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-\frac{c}{k-1}),\quad\gamma_{2}=2(\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell}-(1-c)) $$

Now, by taking $\lambda$ large enough, one can have $|\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}|<\epsilon$ and $|\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell}|<\epsilon$ . This is possible since both terms are present in the optimization and increasing $\lambda$ would make $w^{*}_{\ell}=0$ a feasible solution. This implies $\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1}\xrightarrow{\lambda\rightarrow\infty}\frac{ck}{k-1}-1$ . Furthermore, the condition $\sigma\ll\sqrt{n}$ ensures that $\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ and $\mu_{\ell}^{T}w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ stay close. Thus $\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})\xrightarrow{\lambda\rightarrow\infty}0$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle dR=\frac{2\rho k\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})}{n(1-r)(\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{1})}\xrightarrow{\lambda\rightarrow\infty}0 $$

## Appendix H Proof of Theorem 4.6

#### Theorem H.1.

( $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ - Regularization) Under the assumptions (A1)-(A3), the classification error corresponding to $f(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ can be described as follows in the large $\lambda$ regime with probability approaching $1$ as $n\to\infty$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Xi^{2}:=\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}}(k-1)\gamma_{1}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+\gamma_{2}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}))+\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}}(2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(k-1)r+\frac{k}{n}\sigma^{2}(\gamma_{3}^{2}+\gamma_{4}^{2})) \displaystyle R(\Xi):=2Q(\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}) \displaystyle\Delta(\Xi)^{2}:=\frac{\Xi^{2}}{8\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime}+ \displaystyle\frac{4\delta^{2}}{\lambda^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime}+ \displaystyle\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G+\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime}+ \displaystyle\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle\Omega:=\frac{n^{2}}{k^{2}\Xi^{2}}\left[\gamma_{1}^{2}(k-2)(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-1)r)+(\gamma_{1}^{2}+\gamma_{2}^{2})r+2\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+2\frac{k}{n}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}\sigma^{2}\right] $$

#### Proof.

Similar to the $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ case, we proceed by dividing the proof into several steps.

### H.1 Scalarization of $\bar{\phi}_{\lambda}$

Introducing $\delta$ for $\lambda\|w_{\ell}\|_{\infty}$ , we have for arbitrary $\rho>0$

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\lambda\|w_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\leq\delta}\max_{\gamma}\frac{n}{k}\left[\sum_{\mathscr{r}\neq\ell}[\gamma_{\ell,1}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\mathscr{r}}-\frac{c}{k-1})-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,1}^{2}}{4}]+\gamma_{\ell,2}(w_{\ell}^{T}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}-(1-c))-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,2}^{2}}{4}\right]+ \displaystyle+\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell,3}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}a-s)-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,3}^{2}}{4}+\gamma_{\ell,4}(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}w_{\ell}^{T}b-t)-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,4}^{2}}{4}\right]+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}+\delta $$

The optimization over $w_{\ell}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\|w_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\delta}{\lambda}}\frac{n}{k}\left[\gamma_{\ell,1}\sum_{r\neq\ell}\tilde{\mu}_{r}+\gamma_{\ell,2}\tilde{\mu}_{\ell}+\gamma_{\ell,3}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}a+\gamma_{\ell,4}\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}b\right]^{T}w_{\ell}+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}=\min_{\|w_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\delta}{\lambda}}\Psi_{\ell}^{T}w_{\ell}+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2} $$

For the counterpart scalar optimization $\min_{|x|<b}ax+\rho x^{2}$ we have:

$$ \displaystyle x^{*} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}b&\frac{-a}{2\rho}>b\\
\frac{-a}{2\rho}&-b\leq\frac{-a}{2\rho}\leq b\\
-b&\frac{-a}{2\rho}<-b\end{cases} \displaystyle\min_{|x|<b}ax+\rho x^{2} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}ab+\rho b^{2}&\frac{-a}{2\rho}>b\\
\frac{-a^{2}}{4\rho}&-b\leq\frac{-a}{2\rho}\leq b\\
-ab+\rho b^{2}&\frac{-a}{2\rho}<-b\end{cases} $$

Applying to our problem, then for the solution we have:

$$ \displaystyle w^{*}_{\ell,i}=\begin{cases}\frac{\delta}{\lambda}&\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}>\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\\
\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}&-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\leq\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}\leq\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\\
-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}&\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}<-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\end{cases}=\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}-(\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}-\frac{\delta}{\lambda})\mathds{1}(\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}>\frac{\delta}{\lambda})-(\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}+\frac{\delta}{\lambda})\mathds{1}(\frac{-\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}<-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}) $$

Let

$$ \displaystyle R=\mathbb{P}(|\Psi_{\ell}|=\Xi G\geq\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda})=2Q(\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}) $$

All in all

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\|w_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\delta}{\lambda}}\Psi_{\ell}^{T}w_{\ell}+\rho\|w_{\ell}\|^{2}=d\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\mathbb{E}\left[-\Xi G+\rho\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\right]\mathds{1}(\frac{\Xi G}{2\rho}>\frac{\delta}{\lambda})+d\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\mathbb{E}\left[\Xi G+\rho\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\right]\mathds{1}(\frac{\Xi G}{2\rho}<-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}) \displaystyle-\frac{d}{4\rho}\mathbb{E}\Xi^{2}G^{2}\mathds{1}(-\frac{\delta}{\lambda}\leq\frac{\Xi G}{2\rho}\leq\frac{\delta}{\lambda})= \displaystyle\frac{Rd\delta^{2}\rho}{\lambda^{2}}+\frac{d\delta\Xi}{\lambda}\mathbb{E}(-G\mathds{1}(G>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})+G\mathds{1}(G<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}))-\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho}\mathbb{E}G^{2}\mathds{1}(-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}\leq G\leq\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}))= \displaystyle\frac{Rd\delta^{2}\rho}{\lambda^{2}}-\frac{d\delta\Xi}{\lambda}\mathbb{E}|G|\mathds{1}(|G|>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})-\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho}\mathbb{E}G^{2}\mathds{1}(-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}\leq G\leq\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})= \displaystyle\frac{Rd\delta^{2}\rho}{\lambda^{2}}-\frac{2d\delta\Xi}{\lambda\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{2\rho^{2}\delta^{2}}{\Xi^{2}\lambda^{2}})-\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho}\left[1-2Q(\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})-\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}\exp(-\frac{2\rho^{2}\delta^{2}}{\Xi^{2}\lambda^{2}})\right]= \displaystyle\frac{Rd\delta^{2}\rho}{\lambda^{2}}-\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho}-\frac{d\delta\Xi}{\lambda\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{2\rho^{2}\delta^{2}}{\Xi^{2}\lambda^{2}})+\frac{Rd\Xi^{2}}{4\rho} $$

Where we had by definition $\Xi=\frac{n}{k}\sqrt{(k-1)\gamma_{\ell,1}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n}+(k-2)r)+\gamma_{\ell,2}^{2}(1+\frac{k\sigma^{2}}{n})+2\gamma_{\ell,1}\gamma_{\ell,2}(k-1)r+\frac{k}{n}\sigma^{2}(\gamma_{\ell,3}^{2}+\gamma_{\ell,4}^{2})}$ Summarizing, the objective is:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\delta\geq 0}\max_{\gamma_{\ell,1},\gamma_{\ell,2},\gamma_{\ell,3},\gamma_{\ell,4}}\frac{n}{k}\left[-c\gamma_{\ell,1}-(k-1)\frac{\gamma_{\ell,1}^{2}}{4}-(1-c)\gamma_{\ell,2}-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,2}^{2}}{4}-s\gamma_{\ell,3}-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,3}^{2}}{4}-t\gamma_{\ell,4}-\frac{\gamma_{\ell,4}^{2}}{4}\right]+\delta \displaystyle+\frac{Rd\delta^{2}\rho}{\lambda^{2}}-(1-R)\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho}-\frac{d\delta\Xi}{\lambda\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{2\rho^{2}\delta^{2}}{\Xi^{2}\lambda^{2}}) $$

### H.2 Derivation of the classification error

For the classification error similar to the previous case, we tackle the problem by determining $\|w^{*}_{\ell}-w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|$ and $\mu_{\ell}^{T}(w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}-w^{*}_{\ell})$ . To start off, we have for $\|w^{*}_{\ell}-w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|w^{*}_{\ell}-w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}=d\mathbb{E}(w^{*}_{\ell,i}-w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime},i})^{2}=d\mathbb{E}(\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}-\frac{\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}}{2\rho})^{2}\mathds{1}(|\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}|<\frac{\delta}{\lambda},|\frac{\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}}{2\rho}|<\frac{\delta}{\lambda})+ \displaystyle+2d\mathbb{E}(\frac{\delta}{\lambda}+\frac{\delta}{\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(-\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}>\frac{\delta}{\lambda},-\frac{\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}}{2\rho}<-\frac{\delta}{\lambda})+2d\mathbb{E}(\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}+\frac{\delta}{\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(|\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}|<\frac{\delta}{\lambda},-\frac{\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}}{2\rho}>\frac{\delta}{\lambda})+ \displaystyle+2d\mathbb{E}(\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}-\frac{\delta}{\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(|\frac{\Psi_{\ell,i}}{2\rho}|<\frac{\delta}{\lambda},-\frac{\Psi_{\ell^{\prime},i}}{2\rho}<-\frac{\delta}{\lambda})= \displaystyle d\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}}\mathbb{E}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\mathds{1}(|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},|G^{\prime}|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})+8d\frac{\delta^{2}}{\lambda^{2}}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(-G>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},-G^{\prime}<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})+ \displaystyle+2d\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}}\mathbb{E}(G+\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},-G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})+2d\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}}\mathbb{E}(G-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},-G^{\prime}<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}) $$

Expanding each term

$$ \displaystyle d\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}}\mathbb{E}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\mathds{1}(|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},|G^{\prime}|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})=\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{8\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle 8d\frac{\delta^{2}}{\lambda^{2}}\mathbb{E}\mathds{1}(-G>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},-G^{\prime}<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})=\frac{4d\delta^{2}}{\lambda^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} $$

$$ \displaystyle 2d\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}}\mathbb{E}(G+\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},-G^{\prime} \displaystyle>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})= \displaystyle\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G+\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} \displaystyle 2d\frac{\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}}\mathbb{E}(G-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})^{2}\mathds{1}(|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda},-G^{\prime} \displaystyle<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda})= \displaystyle\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} $$

Combining all of the terms implies

$$ \displaystyle\|w^{*}_{\ell}-w^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}}\|^{2}=\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{8\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{|G^{\prime}|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G-G^{\prime})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime}+ \displaystyle\frac{4d\delta^{2}}{\lambda^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{G<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime}+ \displaystyle\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}<-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G+\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime}+ \displaystyle\frac{d\Xi^{2}}{4\rho^{2}\pi\sqrt{1-\Omega^{2}}}\int_{|G|<\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}\int_{G^{\prime}>\frac{2\rho\delta}{\Xi\lambda}}(G-\frac{2\rho\delta}{\lambda\Xi})^{2}\exp(-\frac{G^{2}+G^{{}^{\prime}2}-2\Omega GG^{\prime}}{2(1-\Omega^{2})})dGdG^{\prime} $$

**Authors:** Danil Akhtiamov∗ Affiliation: Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences Caltech, Pasadena, CA dakhtiam@caltech.edu Reza Ghane∗ Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering Caltech, Pasadena, CA rghanekh@caltech.edu Babak Hassibi Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering Caltech, Pasadena, CA hassibi@caltech.edu

## Abstract

The Randomized Singular Value Decomposition (RSVD) is a widely used algorithm for efficiently computing low-rank approximations of large matrices, without the need to construct a full-blown SVD. Of interest, of course, is the approximation error of RSVD compared to the optimal low-rank approximation error obtained from the SVD. While the literature provides various upper and lower error bounds for RSVD, in this paper we derive precise asymptotic expressions that characterize its approximation error as the matrix dimensions grow to infinity. Our expressions depend only on the singular values of the matrix, and we evaluate them for two important matrix ensembles: those with power law and bilevel singular value distributions. Our results aim to quantify the gap between the existing theoretical bounds and the actual performance of RSVD. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to polynomial-filtered RSVD, deriving performance characterizations that provide insights into optimal filter selection.

## I Introduction

The task of finding a low-rank approximation of a matrix lies at the cornerstone of many computational problems in data science and signal processing. For example, principal component analysis [7], latent semantic indexing [2] and collaborative filtering [8] all fundamentally rely on extracting the dominant singular values and vectors from large-scale matrices. However, as modern datasets grow to unprecedented scales, traditional deterministic algorithms for computing the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) face prohibitive computational and memory constraints. Randomized Singular Value Decomposition (RSVD) [5, 11] has emerged as a powerful alternative, leveraging randomized sampling techniques to compute decent low-rank approximations with dramatically reduced computational complexity. By exploiting the inherent low-rank structure present in many real-world matrices, RSVD achieves approximation errors comparable to deterministic methods, while reducing the time complexity from $O(dn\min(d,n))$ to $O(dnk)$ , where $n$ and $d$ are the dimensions of the matrix, and $k$ is the rank of the approximation. In this work, we develop a novel analysis of RSVD performance and its polynomial-filtered generalizations using Gaussian Comparison Inequalities [3, 4]. We derive exact asymptotic expressions for the approximation error that enable us to quantify the tightness of existing theoretical bounds and provide insights into optimal filter selection. Our precise characterizations not only illuminate the strengths and limitations of current theoretical guarantees but also enable us to improve upon existing upper bounds. By comparing our results with bounds from the literature, we provide a more complete picture of RSVD behavior in practice.

## II Preliminaries

### II-A Randomized SVD

The RSVD algorithm, presented in [5], relies on the idea of Gaussian sketching and works as follows:

```
Input: Matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , $k\leq\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})$
Output: Approximation $\hat{\mathbf{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with $\operatorname{rank}(\hat{\mathbf{A}})\leq k$
• Sample $\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ i.i.d. from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ . • Define $\mathbf{Y}:=\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega}$ . • Take QR-decomposition $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ , where $\mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ . • Define and output $\hat{\mathbf{A}}:=\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A})$ .

```

The following generalization of Algorithm 1, that applies a polynomial filter to $\mathbf{A}$ first, is usually used in practice:

```
Input: Matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , $k\leq\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{A})$ , polynomial filter $\chi(\mathbf{A})=c_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{p}c_{j}\mathbf{(AA^{T})}^{j-1}\mathbf{A}$
Output: Approximation $\hat{\mathbf{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with $\mathrm{rank}(\hat{\mathbf{A}})\leq k$
• Sample $\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ i.i.d. from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ . • Polynomial filtering: Compute $\mathbf{Y}:=\chi(\mathbf{A})\bm{\Omega}$ – Initialize $\mathbf{Y}:=c_{0}\bm{\Omega}$ – Initialize $\mathbf{Z}:=\bm{\Omega}$ // Stores $(\mathbf{A}{\mathbf{A}^{T}})^{j-1}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega}$ – For $j=1$ , find $\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega}$ – For $j=2$ to $p$ : * $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}:=\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{Z}$ * $\mathbf{Z}:=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ // Now $\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{(AA^{T})}^{j-1}\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega}$ * $\mathbf{Y}:=\mathbf{Y}+c_{j}\mathbf{Z}$ • Take QR-decomposition $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ , where $\mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ • Define and output $\hat{\mathbf{A}}:=\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A})$ .

```

The core intuition behind Algorithm 1 is that many important real-world matrices are ”approximately low-rank”. To approximate a matrix $\mathbf{A}$ , which is ”approximately rank $r$ ”, one usually takes $k>r$ in Algorithm 1 to build in tolerance for the algorithm’s inherent approximation error. The rank $r$ is usually referred to as target rank in the literature. To avoid confusion, we would like to highlight that the actual rank of the approximation returned by Algorithm 1 is $k$ rather than $r$ .

As for Algorithm 2, note that $\chi(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{A}$ recovers Algorithm 1. Further intuition is that the polynomial $\chi$ acts as a spectral filter, amplifying dominant singular values while suppressing smaller ones. The choice of $\chi$ can be tailored to the spectral properties of $\mathbf{A}$ , but in this work we mainly concentrate on $\chi(\mathbf{A})=(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{T})^{q}\mathbf{A}$ after deriving the main theorem.

### II-B Related Works

As mentioned in the abstract, the main advantage of the present paper is that its results are tight in the asymptotic regime. The purpose of this section is to elucidate the significance of our results compared to the existing results in the literature.

The seminal work of [5] established approximation error bounds for various randomized low-rank matrix approximations with respect to different matrix norms. More recently, [11] provided simplified analyses yielding cleaner bounds, that can be stated as follows in the case of the Frobenius norm:

#### Theorem 1 (Theorem 8.1 in [11]).

Denote the output of Algorithm 1 for input $\mathbf{A}$ and Gaussian $\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ by $\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})$ and consider an arbitrary $r<k-1$ . It holds that:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\|\mathbf{A}-\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})\|_{F}^{2}\leq\left(1+\frac{r}{k-r-1}\right)\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}^{2} $$

The work of [12] approached the problem from a different angle, establishing worst-case lower bounds. We do not quote the exact statement from [12] to avoid confusion, as the approximation error in [12] is measured with respect to the operator norm. However, we believe that their results can be transferred to the case of the Frobenius norm with minor adjustments. To give a flavor of their main result, they constructed examples of matrices $\mathbf{A}$ , for which the bounds from [5] match the actual performance up to a multiplicative factor of $1-\epsilon$ for any $\epsilon>0$ . This result demonstrates that the upper bounds of [5] cannot be improved for all $\mathbf{A}$ simultaneously.

Our results differ from these prior works in several ways:

- 1. Asymptotic exactness vs. upper bounds: While previous works provide upper bounds (and matching lower bounds in worst case), we establish asymptotic equivalences.

- 2. Full spectral characterization: The bound in Theorem 1 depends only on the tail sum $\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}^{2}$ . In contrast, our implicit characterization involves all singular values $\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{m}$ , capturing how the entire spectral distribution affects the approximation error. This gives a more nuanced picture: two matrices with the same tail sum can have different approximation errors depending on their full spectra.

- 3. Unified framework for filtered variants: While previous analyses treat different algorithmic variants separately, Theorem 3 provides a unified framework. By introducing polynomial filters $\chi$ , we can analyze many algorithms simultaneously.

- 4. Instance-specific vs. worst-case analysis: The lower bounds of [12] are worst-case results. Our results are instance-specific, providing the exact asymptotic error for any given singular value distribution.

## III Main Results

We would like to derive asymptotic predictions for the performance of the RSVD. This requires the following definitions:

#### Definition 1 (RSVD Admissible Sequence).

We call an RSVD admissible sequence any sequence of the form $\{(n_{i},d_{i},m_{i},k_{i},\mathbf{A}^{(i)})\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ , where $\mathbf{A}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d_{i}}$ and $k_{i}\leq\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}^{(i)})=m_{i}$ are such that $k_{i}\to\infty$ . We will denote the non-zero singular values of $\mathbf{A}^{(i)}$ by $\sigma_{1}^{{i}},\dots,\sigma_{m_{i}}^{{i}}$ .

#### Definition 2 (Asymptotic Equivalence).

Given two sequences $\{a_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\{b_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ , we say that they are asymptotically equivalent if $\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}}=1$ . We denote this by $a_{i}\sim b_{i}$ .

For notational brevity, we shall henceforth drop the index $i$ and write $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ to denote a generic element of the ensemble, whose singular values are $\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{m}$ , with the understanding that all statements refer to the asymptotic regime as the matrix dimensions grow. We will drop the index $i$ from the dimensions too.

### III-A Main Theorems

In this section we characterize precisely the approximation error of RSVD with and without polynomial filters.

#### Theorem 2 (Asymptotic Performance of RSVD).

Let $(n,d,m,k,\mathbf{A})$ be an RSVD admissible sequence. Define $\tilde{\Theta}$ as the unique positive solution of

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{\sigma^{2}_{j}}{\tilde{\Theta}+k\sigma^{2}_{j}}=1 $$

Denote the output of Algorithm 1 with a Gaussian matrix $\bm{\Omega}$ applied to $\mathbf{A}$ by $\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})$ . Then the following asymptotic equivalence holds:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\|\mathbf{A}-\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})\|_{F}^{2}\sim\tilde{\Theta} $$

We require the following formal definition of the polynomial filters.

#### Definition 3 (Polynomial filters).

For the purposes of the present work, a filter is an arbitrary polynomial $\chi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ . Given a matrix $\mathbf{X}$ with SVD decomposition $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}$ , we define $\chi(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{U}\chi(\bm{\Sigma})\mathbf{V}$ , where $\chi(\bm{\Sigma})$ is applied element wise to each element of the diagonal.

#### Theorem 3.

Let $(n,d,m,k,\mathbf{A})$ be an RSVD admissible sequence and $\chi$ be a filter. Define $\theta_{0}$ and $\tilde{\Theta}$ as the unique positive numbers satisfying:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{1+\theta_{0}\chi(\sigma_{j})^{2}} \displaystyle=m-k \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{\sigma_{j}^{2}}{1+\theta_{0}\chi(\sigma_{j})^{2}} \displaystyle=\tilde{\Theta} $$

Denote the output of Algorithm 2 with a Gaussian matrix $\bm{\Omega}$ applied to $\mathbf{A}$ by $\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})$ . Then the following asymptotic equivalence holds :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\|\mathbf{A}-\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})\|_{F}^{2}\sim\tilde{\Theta} $$

#### Remark 1.

It should be noted that the expression we get for the approximation error for $\chi(x)=x$ in Theorem 3 is not the same as the expression resulting from Theorem 2. It can actually be shown that the resulting expressions are equivalent, but we prefer to keep the current form of Theorem 2, as the corresponding equation appears simpler.

### III-B Implications

Define

$$ \displaystyle C=C(k,r,m):=\frac{(m-k)k}{(m-r)(k-r)} $$

The following propositions give asymptotic upper bounds for the approximation error of the RSVD in terms of an arbitrary $r<k$ . Note that these bounds are marginally better than Theorem 1 since $r<k$ .

#### Proposition 1.

In terms of the notation from Theorem 2, the following holds:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=k+1}^{m}\sigma_{j}^{2}\leq\tilde{\Theta}\leq C\sum_{j=r+1}^{m}\sigma_{j}^{2} $$

Note that the lower bound in Proposition 1 follows readily from Eckart-Young theorem. The following result provides an asymptotic upper bound for the approximation error of arbitrary polynomial filters.

#### Proposition 2.

In terms of the notation from Theorem 3, the following holds:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\Theta}\leq\sum_{j=r+1}^{m}\sigma_{j}^{2}+\frac{C}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{r}\frac{\sigma_{j}^{2}}{\chi(\sigma_{j})^{2}}\cdot\sum_{j=r+1}^{m}\chi(\sigma_{j})^{2} $$

It turns out, in the case of the Bilevel Ensemble and the Power law Ensemble, the asymptotic error and the structure of an optimal filter can characterized explicitly as follows.

#### Corollary 1.

- • (Bilevel Ensemble). Assume that $\sigma_{1}=\dots=\sigma_{r}=a$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{m}=b$ , with $a>b$ . Then the approximation error would be $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\|\mathbf{A}-\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})\|_{F}^{2}$ (1) $\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2}\Bigl((r-k)a^{2}+(m-r-k)b^{2}+$ $\displaystyle\sqrt{((r-k)a^{2}+(m-r-k)b^{2})^{2}+4a^{2}b^{2}(m-k)}\Bigr)$ In this setting for $k\geq r+1$ , the optimal polynomial filter is of form $\chi(\cdot):=(\cdot)^{q}$ where $q\rightarrow\infty$ and yields an error of $(m-k)b^{2}$ , the fundamental lower bound from Proposition 1.

- • (Power law Ensemble). Assume that $\sigma_{i}=i^{-\alpha}$ , then $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\|\mathbf{A}-\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\bm{\Omega})\|_{F}^{2}\sim\frac{1}{\Bigl(k\text{sinc}(\frac{\pi}{2\alpha})\Bigr)^{2\alpha}}$ (2) $\displaystyle\text{where }\text{sinc}(x)=\frac{\sin(x)}{x}$ In this setting, $\chi(\cdot):=(\cdot)^{q}$ where $q\rightarrow\infty$ yields an error of $\sum_{i=k+1}^{m}i^{-2\alpha}$ , the fundamental lower bound from Proposition 1.

#### Remark 2.

For the bilevel ensemble, the upper bound in Theorem 1 yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{k-1}{k-r-1}(m-r)b^{2} $$

whereas, assuming $k=o(m)$ and $\frac{a}{b}=\Theta(1)$ , (1) asymptotically equals

$$ (m-k)b^{2} $$

If the difference $k-r$ is constant, we conclude that our prediction (1) is tighter than (3) by a factor of $\Theta(k)$ .

#### Remark 3.

For the power law ensemble, the upper bound in Theorem 1 yields approximately

$$ \displaystyle\frac{k-1}{k-r-1}\cdot\frac{1}{2\alpha-1}\cdot\frac{1}{r^{2\alpha-1}} $$

The bound (4) is $\Theta(k^{2})$ - fold greater than (2) if the oversampling $k-r$ is constant and $\Theta(k)$ - fold greater if $r$ is a finite fraction of $k$ .

## IV Our Approach

### IV-A Variational reformulation

The following key lemma provides a variation formulation for the RSVD algorithm which allows us to apply Gaussian Comparison Inequalities[3, 4].

#### Lemma 1.

Let $\chi$ be a polynomial filter and assume that $\mathrm{rank}(\chi(\mathbf{A})\bm{\Omega})=k$ under the notation of Algorithm 2. Then the output of Algorithm 2 can be found as $\hat{\mathbf{A}}=\chi(\mathbf{A})\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}$ , where $\mathbf{B}$ is defined uniquely via the following objective:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}}\|\mathbf{A}-\chi(\mathbf{A})\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2} $$

When $\chi(x)=x$ , this description captures the output of Algorithm 1.

#### Remark 4.

Define the approximation error of Algorithm 2 as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\|\mathbf{A}-\hat{\mathbf{A}}\|_{F}^{2} $$

We see from Lemma 1 that (5) equals

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}}\min_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}}\|\mathbf{A}-\chi(\mathbf{A})\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2} $$

### IV-B Proof of Theorem 2

We present the proof of Theorem 2 below. The proof of Theorem 3 follows the same steps and is omitted here due to the lack of space.

#### Proof of Theorem 2 .

Consider the truncated SVD decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V},\text{ where }m=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}),\;\bm{\Sigma}=\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}\sigma_{i}\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{T}, \displaystyle\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d},\quad\mathbf{U}^{T}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}_{m}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^{T} $$

Due to rotational invariance of the Frobenius norm we have:

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\|\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{U}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\|\bm{\Sigma}-\bm{\Sigma}(\mathbf{V}\bm{\Omega})(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{V}^{T})\|_{F}^{2} $$

Noting that $\mathbf{V}\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ is also i.i.d. standard Gaussian and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{V})=m$ , we redefine $\bm{\Omega}:=\mathbf{V}\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ , $\mathbf{B}:=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{V}^{T}$ and arrive at the following:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}}\min_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times m}}\|\bm{\Sigma}-\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2} $$

Introducing the Fenchel dual variable $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ for the quadratic loss $\|\cdot\|_{F}^{2}$ we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}} \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times m}}\max_{\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}}\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{C}^{T}\left(\bm{\Sigma}-\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\right)\right)-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}\|_{F}^{2}}{4} $$

Denote the optimization variables

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{C} \displaystyle=(\mathbf{C}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{C}_{m}),\quad\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} \displaystyle\mathbf{B} \displaystyle=(\mathbf{B}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{B}_{m}),\quad\mathbf{B}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} $$

Expression (6) decomposes as:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}}\min_{\mathbf{B}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{B}}}\max_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\mathbf{C}_{i}^{T}\left(\sigma_{i}\mathbf{e}_{i}-\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}_{i}\right)-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|^{2}}{4} $$

Define the constraint sets

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{B}}:=\Bigl\{\mathbf{B}_{i}:\|\mathbf{B}_{i}\|\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}-\sqrt{k}}\frac{\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{A})}{\sigma_{m}(\mathbf{A})}\Bigr\} \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{C}}:=\{\mathbf{C}_{i}:\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|\leq\sigma_{i}\} $$

Consider the following pair of optimizations:

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{i}(\bm{\Omega}):=\max_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{C}}}\min_{\mathbf{B}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{B}}}\mathbf{C}_{i}^{T}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}_{i}+\sigma_{i}\mathbf{C}_{ii}-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|^{2}}{4} $$

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{i}(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{h}):=\max_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{C}}}\min_{\mathbf{B}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{B}}} \displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{i}^{T}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{g}\|\mathbf{B}_{i}\|+\mathbf{B}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{h}\|\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{C}_{i}\| \displaystyle+\sigma_{i}\mathbf{C}_{ii}-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|^{2}}{4} $$

We further define $\phi^{HW}_{i}(\mathbf{h}):=\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{1+\theta_{\mathbf{h}}\sigma_{i}^{2}}$ and $c_{i}:=\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{1+\theta\sigma_{i}^{2}}$ for $i\in[m]$ where $\theta_{\mathbf{h}}$ and $\theta$ are defined via

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{1+\theta_{\mathbf{h}}\sigma_{j}^{2}} \displaystyle=m-\|\mathbf{h}\|^{2} \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{1+\theta\sigma_{j}^{2}} \displaystyle=m-k $$

Going back to (6), we observe that it can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}}\min_{\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times m}}\|\bm{\Sigma}-\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2}= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\max_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\min_{\mathbf{B}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}}\mathbf{C}_{i}^{T}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}_{i}+\sigma_{i}\mathbf{C}_{ii}-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|^{2}}{4} $$

From Lemma 2,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}}\max_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\min_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}}\mathbf{C}_{i}^{T}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}_{i}+\sigma_{i}\mathbf{C}_{ii}-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|^{2}}{4} \displaystyle\sim\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}}\Phi_{i}(\bm{\Omega}) $$

Indeed, according to Lemma 2, the optimal $\mathbf{C}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{B}_{i}$ belong in the sets $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{C}}$ and $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{B}}$ with probability approaching $1$ as $m\to\infty$ and the objective is bounded outside of these sets according to the same lemma. In Lemma 3 located in the Appendix, we prove that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}}\Phi_{i}(\bm{\Omega})-c_{i}\right|\leq 2\left|\mathbb{E}\phi_{i}(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{h})-c_{i}\right| $$

We then proceed to apply the triangle inequality:

$$ \displaystyle 2\left|\mathbb{E}\phi_{i}(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{h})-c_{i}\right|\leq \displaystyle 2|\mathbb{E}\phi_{i}(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{h})-\mathbb{E}\phi^{HW}_{i}(\mathbf{h})| \displaystyle\quad+2\left|\mathbb{E}\phi^{HW}_{i}(\mathbf{h})-c_{i}\right| $$

After that, we prove that $\mathbb{E}\phi_{i}(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{h})\sim\mathbb{E}\phi^{HW}_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ and $\mathbb{E}\phi^{HW}_{i}(\mathbf{h})\sim c_{i}$ in the Appendix, in Lemma 4 and Lemma 5 respectively. Hence, it suffices to prove that $\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}=\tilde{\Theta}$ . The latter is a straightforward algebra verification:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}=\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{1+\theta\sigma_{i}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(1-\frac{1}{1+\theta\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right)=\frac{k}{\theta} $$

It only remains to check that $\tilde{\Theta}=\frac{k}{\theta}$ , which is true since, by definition of $\theta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\frac{k}{\theta}+k\sigma_{i}^{2}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\theta\sigma_{i}^{2}}{1+\theta\sigma_{i}^{2}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(1-\frac{1}{1+\theta\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right)=1 $$

∎

We sample matrices with power-law and bilevel spectra and plot the error of the RSVD (Algorithm 1) and the RSVD with a polynomial filter corresponding to the power iteration method (Algorithm 2) with $\mathbf{A}\mapsto(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{T})^{q}\mathbf{A}$ , against the value of $k$ along with the corresponding theoretical prediction provided in Corollary 1. As a baseline, we also plotted the fundamental lower bound and also the upper bound from 1 to compare the performance of various polynomial filters and the best achievable error:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=k+1}^{m}\sigma_{j}^{2}\leq\tilde{\Theta}\leq C\sum_{j=r+1}^{m}\sigma_{j}^{2} $$

The results and the details of the ensembles are presented in Figures 1a, 1b. We observe a close match between the theoretical predictions and the empirical errors for large enough values of $k$ . ## VI Conclusion and Future Work

We have derived exact asymptotic characterizations for RSVD performance that capture the full spectral structure of the data matrix and naturally extend to polynomial-filtered variants. Our results complement existing literature by bridging the gap between worst-case guarantees and actual performance: while prior work establishes what can be guaranteed in general, our analysis reveals what actually occurs for specific problem instances in the large-scale limit. Our approach opens several avenues for future research. The framework developed here can be extended to investigate other properties of RSVD approximation error, including finite-sample corrections to our asymptotic results and the universality of approximation error across different choices of sketching matrices $\bm{\Omega}$ . These directions would further enhance our understanding of RSVD behavior beyond the asymptotic regime and across diverse randomization strategies.

## VIII Appendix

### VIII-A Technical Lemmata

#### Proof of Lemma 1.

Let $\mathbf{Y}=\chi(\mathbf{A})\bm{\Omega}$ . The optimization problem is a least squares problem. The optimal solution is:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{B}^{*}=(\mathbf{Y}^{T}\mathbf{Y})^{-1}\mathbf{Y}^{T}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Y}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A} $$

Using the QR decomposition:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{Y}^{\dagger} \displaystyle=(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R})^{\dagger}=\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{T} $$

Therefore:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{B}^{*} \displaystyle=\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A} $$

The approximation given by this optimal $\mathbf{B}^{*}$ is:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{B}^{*}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A} $$

∎

For all subsequent lemmas we operate under the notation and assumptions of Theorem 2 and Theorem 3.

#### Lemma 2.

Let $\mathbf{B}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{C}_{i}$ be the solutions to the optimization problem:

$$ \min_{\mathbf{B}_{i}}\|\bm{\Sigma}_{i}-\bm{\Sigma}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}_{i}\|^{2} $$

Then,

1. With probability at least $1-e^{-\frac{(\sqrt{d}-\sqrt{k})^{2}}{8}}$ , it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathbf{B}^{*}\|\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}-\sqrt{k}}\kappa(\mathbf{A}) $$

where $\kappa(\mathbf{A})=\frac{\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A})}$ is the condition number of $\mathbf{A}$ .

2. The following always holds:

$$ \|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|_{2}\leq\sigma_{i} $$

#### Proof.

1. From Lemma 1, we have $\mathbf{B}^{*}=\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A}$ . Using the submultiplicativity property:

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathbf{B}^{*}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{R}^{-1}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{R}^{-1}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2} $$

Applying standard RMT results to $\sigma_{\min}(\bm{\Omega})$ we are done since:

$$ \|\mathbf{R}^{-1}\|_{2}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{R})}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A}\bm{\Omega})}\leq\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A})}\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(\bm{\Omega})} $$

2. Plug in the feasible solution $\mathbf{B}_{i}=0$ .

∎

Then we obtain:

#### Lemma 3.

Let $\gamma\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{i}(\bm{\Omega},\gamma):=\max_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{C}}}\min_{\mathbf{C}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{B}}} \displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{i}^{T}\bm{\Omega}\mathbf{B}_{i}+\sigma_{i}\mathbf{C}_{ii} \displaystyle-\frac{\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\|^{2}}{4}+\gamma\|\mathbf{C}_{i}\| $$

The following inequalities hold for any $c,t\in\mathbb{R}$ :

$$ \displaystyle 1.\quad\mathbb{P}\left(|\Phi_{i}(\bm{\Omega})-c|>t\right)\leq 2\mathbb{P}\left(|\Psi_{i}(\bm{\Omega},\gamma)-c|>t\right) $$
